lessons.title: Homeostasis and Feedback Mechanisms
lessons.notes_html:
Homeostasis

Homeostasis is a self-regulating process by which biological systems maintain stability while adjusting to the changing conditions. It is the overall process of keeping the internal environment stable. Osmoregulation and excretion are only parts of it that help in maintaining it.

Why physiological integration of the internal environment is important

Cells can work properly only when temperature, pH, water, salts and nutrients around them stay within narrow limits. Physiological integration coordinates organs such as the kidney, liver, lungs and endocrine glands so that this internal environment remains stable. Without it, enzymes would fail and the organism could not survive changes in the external environment.

Negative feedback and positive feedback

  • Negative feedback: counteracts the change and restores the stable condition. It keeps most body variables stable by reversing any change.
  • Positive feedback: does not maintain a stable, homeostatic condition; rather it intensifies the change that is happening to the body. It amplifies the original change instead of reversing it, and rapidly completes certain processes such as blood clotting and childbirth.
FeedbackEffect on changeRole
Negative feedbackCounteracts and reverses the changeKeeps most body variables stable
Positive feedbackAmplifies and intensifies the changeRapidly completes processes such as blood clotting and childbirth

Balance between the two feedback mechanisms

It is important that positive and negative feedback mechanisms counteract upon each other. Negative feedback keeps most body variables stable by reversing any change, while positive feedback rapidly completes certain processes such as blood clotting and childbirth. The two must balance and counteract each other so that a useful positive response does not continue endlessly and upset homeostasis. This balance allows both stability and timely, controlled change in the body.

mcqs.why: Homeostasis is the overall self-regulating process that keeps the internal environment stable, while osmoregulation and excretion are only parts of it.

mcqs.q: Positive feedback differs from negative feedback because positive feedback:
options: Intensifies the change that is happening to the body
mcqs.why: Positive feedback does not maintain a stable condition; it amplifies and intensifies the original change instead of reversing it.

mcqs.q: Blood clotting and childbirth are examples of processes rapidly completed by:
mcqs.why: Positive feedback rapidly completes certain processes such as blood clotting and childbirth by amplifying the change rather than reversing it.

mcqs.why: Negative feedback keeps most body variables stable by reversing any change, whereas positive feedback is the mechanism that rapidly completes processes.

Enzymes would fail and the organism could not survive external changes
mcqs.why: Without a stable internal environment enzymes would fail, and the organism could not survive changes in the external environment.

So that a useful positive response does not continue endlessly and upset homeostasis

mcqs.why: The two mechanisms must balance so a useful positive response does not continue endlessly and upset homeostasis, allowing both stability and controlled change.

Parts of homeostasis that help in maintaining it
mcqs.why: Osmoregulation and excretion are only parts of homeostasis that help in maintaining the overall stability of the internal environment.

lessons.title: Osmoregulation in Animals
lessons.notes_html:
Osmoregulation

Osmoregulation is a part of homeostasis that helps in maintaining it by keeping the internal osmotic concentration constant. Aquatic osmoregulators overcome their osmoregulatory problems by excretion and active ion transport.

Ionocytes in freshwater organisms

Fresh water organisms have specialized cells located in their gills and in skin which actively extract Na+, Cl- and Ca+ from external medium and excrete H+ or basic HCO3- for acid base balance in the body fluids. These cells are called ionocytes.

  • Ionocytes: the specialized ion-transporting cells of gills and skin in freshwater animals. They take up needed ions from the dilute surroundings and remove H+ or HCO3- to keep acid-base balance.

How aquatic osmoregulators overcome osmoregulatory problems

  • Freshwater animals: face continuous entry of water and loss of salts, so they excrete large amounts of dilute urine and actively absorb Na+, Cl- and other ions through ionocytes in the gills and skin.
  • Marine animals: face the opposite problem of water loss and salt gain, so they drink seawater, excrete excess salt through gills and produce very little concentrated urine.
Animal groupProblemResponse
Freshwater animalsContinuous entry of water and loss of saltsExcrete large amounts of dilute urine; actively absorb Na+, Cl- and other ions through ionocytes in the gills and skin
Marine animalsWater loss and salt gainDrink seawater, excrete excess salt through gills and produce very little concentrated urine

In both cases excretion and active ion transport keep the internal osmotic concentration constant.

mcqs.q: Osmoregulation helps in maintaining homeostasis by keeping constant the:
mcqs.why: Osmoregulation is the part of homeostasis that keeps the internal osmotic concentration constant through excretion and active ion transport.

mcqs.q: Ionocytes in freshwater organisms are located in the:
mcqs.why: Freshwater organisms have specialized ionocytes located in their gills and in the skin, where they actively transport ions.

mcqs.q: Ionocytes actively extract which ions from the external medium?
mcqs.why: Ionocytes actively extract Na+, Cl- and Ca+ from the external medium of freshwater animals, which live in a dilute surrounding.

mcqs.q: For acid-base balance in the body fluids, ionocytes excrete:
mcqs.why: Ionocytes excrete H+ or basic HCO3- so that the acid-base balance of the body fluids of freshwater animals is maintained.

mcqs.q: The main osmoregulatory problem faced by freshwater animals is:
options: Continuous loss of water and gain of salts
Continuous entry of water and loss of salts
Complete absence of salts in the body
mcqs.why: Freshwater animals face continuous entry of water and loss of salts because their surroundings are dilute compared with their body fluids.

mcqs.q: Freshwater animals respond to water entry and salt loss by:
options: Excreting large amounts of dilute urine and actively absorbing ions
Excreting excess salt through the gills
mcqs.why: Freshwater animals excrete large amounts of dilute urine and actively absorb Na+, Cl- and other ions through ionocytes in the gills and skin.

mcqs.q: The main osmoregulatory problem faced by marine animals is:
mcqs.why: Marine animals face the opposite problem to freshwater animals: water loss from the body and gain of salts from the seawater.

mcqs.q: Marine animals overcome water loss and salt gain by:
options: Excreting large amounts of dilute urine
Absorbing ions through ionocytes in the skin
Drinking seawater, excreting excess salt through the gills and producing very little concentrated urine
mcqs.why: Marine animals drink seawater, excrete excess salt through the gills and produce very little concentrated urine, conserving water.

mcqs.q: In both freshwater and marine osmoregulators, the internal osmotic concentration is kept constant by:
mcqs.why: In both cases excretion and active ion transport work together to keep the internal osmotic concentration constant.

mcqs.q: The specialized ion-transporting cells of the gills and skin in freshwater animals are called:
mcqs.why: Ionocytes are the specialized ion-transporting cells of gills and skin in freshwater animals; podocytes are cells of the glomerulus in the kidney.

lessons.title: Excretion and Nitrogenous Wastes
lessons.notes_html:
Excretion

Excretion is a part of homeostasis that helps in maintaining it. Animals excrete different types of excretory waste, and the type of nitrogenous waste depends on the availability of water and the habitat of the animal.

Why animals excrete different types of excretory waste

  • Ammonia: highly toxic but needs much water for its removal, so it is excreted mainly by aquatic animals.
  • Urea: less toxic and needs moderate water, so it is excreted by mammals.
  • Uric acid: almost non-toxic and needs very little water, so it suits birds, reptiles and desert animals.
Nitrogenous wasteToxicityWater needed for removalExcreted mainly by
AmmoniaHighly toxicMuch waterAquatic animals
UreaLess toxicModerate waterMammals
Uric acidAlmost non-toxicVery little waterBirds, reptiles and desert animals

The type of nitrogenous waste depends on the availability of water and the habitat of the animal.

options: The colour of the animal and its speed
The availability of water and the habitat of the animal
The type of food colouring it eats
mcqs.why: The type of nitrogenous waste depends on the availability of water and the habitat of the animal, because each waste needs a different amount of water for removal.

mcqs.why: Ammonia is highly toxic but can be removed safely because aquatic animals have plenty of water available to dilute and wash it out.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is excreted mainly by:
mcqs.why: Ammonia is excreted mainly by aquatic animals, since it is highly toxic and needs much water for its removal.

mcqs.q: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste of mammals because urea is:
options: Highly toxic and needs much water
A solid that needs no water at all
Less toxic and needs only moderate water
mcqs.why: Urea is less toxic than ammonia and needs only moderate water for its removal, so it suits mammals.

mcqs.q: Which nitrogenous waste is almost non-toxic and needs very little water for its removal?
mcqs.why: Uric acid is almost non-toxic and needs very little water for its removal, which is why it suits animals with little available water.

mcqs.why: Uric acid suits birds, reptiles and desert animals because it is almost non-toxic and needs very little water for its removal.

options: Needs very little water for its removal
Needs much water for its removal

mcqs.why: Uric acid needs very little water for its removal, so desert animals can excrete it without losing much of their scarce water.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the water needed to remove nitrogenous wastes is correct?
options: Urea needs more water than ammonia
Uric acid needs the most water of all
All three wastes need exactly the same water
Ammonia needs much water, urea moderate water and uric acid very little water
mcqs.why: Ammonia needs much water, urea needs moderate water and uric acid needs very little water for removal, matching their different toxicities.

mcqs.q: Excretion is described in the notes as:
options: A part of homeostasis that helps in maintaining it
A process found only in aquatic animals
mcqs.why: Excretion is a part of homeostasis that helps in maintaining it, by removing nitrogenous wastes from the body.

mcqs.q: Mammals excrete mainly which nitrogenous waste?
mcqs.why: Mammals excrete urea, which is less toxic than ammonia and needs only a moderate amount of water for its removal.

lessons.title: The Human Kidney and Structure of the Nephron
lessons.notes_html:
The nephron

A nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney, and each kidney contains about a million nephrons. It begins with the renal corpuscle, made of the glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries, surrounded by the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule whose inner layer is formed of podocytes; here ultrafiltration of blood takes place. The filtrate then passes through the proximal convoluted tubule, where most glucose, amino acids, salts and water are reabsorbed, then through the loop of Henle, whose descending and ascending limbs create the counter current gradient, and then through the distal convoluted tubule, where secretion of H+, K+ and drugs and further reabsorption occur. Finally the nephron opens into the collecting duct, which carries urine to the renal pelvis while reabsorbing water under ADH control.

  • Renal corpuscle: made of the glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries, surrounded by the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule; ultrafiltration of blood takes place here.
  • Proximal convoluted tubule: most glucose, amino acids, salts and water are reabsorbed here.
  • Loop of Henle: its descending and ascending limbs create the counter current gradient.
  • Distal convoluted tubule: secretion of H+, K+ and drugs and further reabsorption occur here.
  • Collecting duct: carries urine to the renal pelvis while reabsorbing water under ADH control.

Podocytes and filtration

Podocyte cells are specialized cells of the glomerulus that are wrapped around blood capillaries and play an active role in preventing plasma proteins from entering the urinary ultrafiltrate. Podocytes wrap the glomerular capillaries with their foot processes and form part of the filtration barrier. This barrier allows water and small solutes to pass but holds back plasma proteins and blood cells. The inner layer of Bowman's capsule is formed of podocytes.

Glomerular filtration rate

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is directly proportional to the hydrostatic pressure exerted in glomerulus wall. When hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus rises, more fluid is forced through the filtration membrane, so GFR increases. When the pressure falls, GFR also falls.

Distal convoluted tubule and acid-base balance

The distal convoluted tubule secretes ions such as hydrogen, potassium, and NH3 into the filtrate while reabsorbing the HCO3- from the filtrate. It secretes H+, K+ and ammonia into the filtrate and reabsorbs bicarbonate from it. In this way it plays an important role in acid-base and electrolyte balance.

Counter current mechanism in kidney

The counter current mechanism in the loop of Henle builds a strong osmotic gradient in the medulla, from the cortex towards the inner medulla. This gradient allows water to be drawn out of the collecting duct under the control of ADH. As a result, the kidney can produce urine more concentrated than blood and conserve water when the body needs it.

Urea and the osmotic gradient in inner medulla

Urea is another compound that increases the osmotic gradient in inner medulla. Along with NaCl, urea accumulates in the inner medulla and increases its osmotic gradient. This gradient helps the collecting duct to reabsorb water and produce concentrated urine.

Functions of kidney

The kidney performs several vital functions for homeostasis. It excretes nitrogenous wastes such as urea, excess salts and drugs in urine, regulates the water and osmotic balance of blood, and maintains acid-base balance by secreting H+ and reabsorbing bicarbonate. It also regulates blood pressure through renin and fluid volume control, secretes erythropoietin for red blood cell formation, and activates vitamin D for calcium metabolism.

  • Excretion: excretes nitrogenous wastes such as urea, excess salts and drugs in urine.
  • Water and osmotic balance: regulates the water and osmotic balance of blood.
  • Acid-base balance: maintains acid-base balance by secreting H+ and reabsorbing bicarbonate.
  • Blood pressure: regulates blood pressure through renin and fluid volume control.
  • Red blood cell formation: secretes erythropoietin for red blood cell formation.
  • Calcium metabolism: activates vitamin D for calcium metabolism.

Kidney as an endocrine organ

Besides excretion, the kidney secretes important hormones, so it also acts as an endocrine organ. It produces erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell formation in bone marrow, and renin, which helps regulate blood pressure and salt balance. It also activates vitamin D, which is needed for calcium absorption.

  • Erythropoietin: an important hormone necessary for the synthesis of RBC's, produced by the renal cortex. It is released by the kidney, mainly from the renal cortex, when oxygen in blood falls. It stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells.
  • Renin: helps regulate blood pressure and salt balance.
  • Vitamin D: the kidney activates vitamin D, which is needed for calcium absorption.

mcqs.why: The collecting duct reabsorbs water under ADH control as it carries urine to the renal pelvis, so urine becomes more concentrated.

lessons.title: Kidney Disorders, Failure and Transplant
lessons.notes_html:
How kidney stones are formed

Urine contains dissolved minerals and salts such as calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and uric acid. When urine becomes too concentrated, or these substances increase, they crystallize and gradually deposit in the kidney or urinary tract to form stones. Low water intake, excess salts in diet and urinary infections increase the risk of stone formation.

Lithonephritis

Lithonephritis is the inflammation in kidneys due to irritation of kidney stones. It is the inflammation of the kidney caused by the irritation of kidney stones.

  • Edema: swelling due to fluid.
  • Sarcoma: a cancer.
  • Encephalitis: inflammation of the brain.

Impact if kidneys lose filtering ability

When kidneys lose their filtering ability, urea and other wastes accumulate in the blood and water and salt balance is disturbed. This causes nausea, swelling, high blood pressure, anaemia, weakness and disturbance of acid-base balance. In complete kidney failure the condition becomes life-threatening unless dialysis or transplant is provided.

Causes of kidney failure

Kidney failure may be sudden or gradual and is caused by conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes and high blood pressure, glomerular inflammation, kidney stones, urinary tract obstruction, infections and toxic drugs that damage the nephrons. As filtration fails, wastes and fluids accumulate in the body and disturb blood chemistry.

Treatment of kidney failure

Treatment includes controlling the cause and diet, haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis and continuous renal replacement therapy to artificially filter the blood, and in severe permanent failure, kidney transplant from a suitable donor.

Problems associated with kidney transplant

The main problem is rejection, because the immune system of the recipient recognizes the donor kidney as foreign and attacks it, so immunosuppressive drugs are needed for life. These drugs increase the risk of infections and other side effects. Other problems include shortage of suitable donors, the need for close tissue matching, high cost and possible failure of the transplanted kidney after some years.

  • Rejection: the immune system of the recipient recognizes the donor kidney as foreign and attacks it.
  • Immunosuppressive drugs: needed for life; they increase the risk of infections and other side effects.
  • Other problems: shortage of suitable donors, the need for close tissue matching, high cost and possible failure of the transplanted kidney after some years.

lessons.title: Thermoregulation
lessons.notes_html:
Thermoregulation

Thermoregulation is the regulation of body temperature as part of homeostasis. Body temperature must stay within a suitable limit, and it rises or falls when heat production and heat loss are disturbed.

Hyperthermia

If the surrounding environment becomes hot or a person does strenuous physical activity, the heat produced inside the body raises body temperature above suitable limit; this condition is called hyperthermia. Hyperthermia is the rise of body temperature above the normal suitable limit due to external heat or heavy physical activity.

Hypothermia

Hypothermia is the opposite condition to hyperthermia, in which body temperature falls below normal. It is the condition in which body temperature falls below the normal limit, usually due to prolonged exposure to cold.

ConditionBody temperatureCause
HyperthermiaRises above the normal suitable limitExternal heat or heavy physical activity
HypothermiaFalls below the normal limitUsually prolonged exposure to cold

How body overcomes hypothermia

The body overcomes hypothermia by shivering, which produces heat through rapid muscle contractions, and by constriction of skin blood vessels, which reduces heat loss. Behavioural responses such as seeking shelter and wearing warm clothes also help restore normal temperature.

  • Shivering: produces heat through rapid muscle contractions.
  • Constriction of skin blood vessels: reduces heat loss.
  • Behavioural responses: seeking shelter and wearing warm clothes help restore normal temperature.

lessons.title: Bone Cells, Bone Formation and Cartilage
lessons.notes_html:
Bone cells

Bone is built, maintained and remodelled by different types of bone cells.

  • Osteoclasts: large cells that break down and resorb old bone tissue during growth and remodeling; they tear down bone during the building and remodeling process.
  • Osteoblasts: do the opposite work of osteoclasts and build new bone.
  • Osteocytes: maintain the mature bone.

Periosteal bone collar

During bone formation, as the periosteum calcifies, it gives rise to a thin plate of compact bone called the periosteal bone collar. The periosteum around the shaft calcifies and forms this collar. This collar supports the developing bone and is later thickened as ossification proceeds.

Cartilage and perichondrium

Cartilage is a soft flexible form of connective tissue. It is surrounded by a layer called the perichondrium.

  • Perichondrium: a dense connective tissue layer that covers cartilage externally, nourishes it and helps in its growth and repair.
  • Periosteum: the corresponding covering layer of bone, not of cartilage.

How cartilage is useful for the skeletal system

Cartilage covers the ends of bones at joints, where it reduces friction and absorbs shocks during movement. It also gives shape and flexible support to structures such as the nose, ears and trachea, and in children it forms the model from which bones develop and lengthen. Being soft and flexible, it protects the joints from wear and damage.

Different types of cartilage

  • Hyaline cartilage: glassy and smooth; covers the ends of bones at joints and is found in the nose, trachea and ribs, where it provides support with flexibility.
  • Elastic cartilage: contains many elastic fibers, is highly flexible, and is found in the external ear and epiglottis.
  • Fibrocartilage: contains dense collagen fibers, is the strongest type, and is found in intervertebral discs and the knee, where it resists compression and absorbs shocks.
Type of cartilageFeatures and places
Hyaline cartilageGlassy and smooth; ends of bones at joints, nose, trachea and ribs; support with flexibility
Elastic cartilageMany elastic fibers, highly flexible; external ear and epiglottis
FibrocartilageDense collagen fibers, strongest type; intervertebral discs and knee; resists compression and absorbs shocks

The pelvic girdle

lessons.title: Fracture Repair, Sprains and First Aid for Joint Injuries
lessons.notes_html:
How the healing of a fractured bone is initiated

When a bone fractures, blood vessels in the bone and periosteum are torn, causing pain and bleeding that forms a clot called a hematoma around the broken ends. The pain and swelling signal injury, and the hematoma provides the framework in which repair begins. In the next steps a cartilaginous callus joins the broken ends, which is then replaced by bone and finally remodeled.

Repair process of simple fractures

Repair of a simple fracture takes place in a fixed sequence of steps.

  • Hematoma formation: bleeding from torn vessels forms a hematoma (blood clot) around the broken ends, which seals the area.
  • Callus formation: an internal and external callus of cartilage forms and joins the two sides temporarily.
  • Replacement by bone: the cartilage of the callus is replaced by trabecular (spongy) bone, making the union firm.
  • Bone remodeling stage: osteoclasts remove dead and excess bone and osteoblasts lay down compact bone, restoring the original shape and strength.

In the bone remodeling stage, old bone tissues are removed and replaced with new ones that join both fractured sides. Osteoclasts remove old and dead bone and osteoblasts lay down new bone that firmly joins both fractured sides, and the bone is gradually remodeled to its original shape and strength.

Sprains

A sprain is related to the mild to severe grade of stretching or tearing of a ligament that holds the bones of a joint together. Spasm, tetany and cramps are abnormal conditions of muscles, not of ligaments.

First aid treatment for joint injuries and fractures

  • Keep the part still: the injured part should be kept still and supported, for example with a splint or sling, so that the broken bone or injured joint does not move and cause further damage.
  • Cold packs: can be applied to reduce pain and swelling.
  • Raised limb: the limb may be kept raised.
  • Bandaging: tight bandaging should be avoided.
  • Hospital treatment: the patient should then be taken to hospital promptly for X-ray, proper alignment and plastering or other treatment.

lessons.title: Types of Muscles and Structure of Skeletal Muscle
lessons.notes_html:
Comparison of types of muscles

Type of muscleFeatures
Skeletal musclesAttached to bones, striated and voluntary; produce body movements such as walking and lifting
Smooth musclesFound in the walls of involuntary organs like the gut and blood vessels, non-striated and work automatically
Cardiac muscleFound only in the heart, striated but involuntary; contracts rhythmically throughout life without fatigue

Cardiac muscle and syncytium

The heart muscles are arranged in a branching network where cells are joined together and make a syncytium. Cardiac muscle cells branch and are joined end to end by intercalated discs, so the whole tissue works as a single functional unit called a syncytium. This allows the heart to contract in a coordinated wave.

Structure of skeletal muscles

A skeletal muscle is made of bundles of long muscle fibers held together by connective tissue layers.

  • Muscle fiber: each individual fiber is covered by the endomysium, and its cell membrane is the sarcolemma.
  • Fascicle: muscle fibers are gathered in many groups; each group of fibers is called a fascicle, which is surrounded by a membrane called the perimysium.
  • Whole muscle: covered by the epimysium.
Layer / membraneWhat it covers
EndomysiumIndividual fibers
PerimysiumEach fascicle, a bundle of muscle fibers
EpimysiumThe whole muscle
SarcolemmaThe cell membrane of a fiber

Ultra structure of skeletal muscle fiber

Under the sarcolemma, each fiber contains many rod-like myofibrils made of repeating units called sarcomeres, which are the units of contraction. Each sarcomere has thick myosin filaments in the A band and thin actin filaments in the I band, separated by Z lines, and their sliding over each other shortens the fiber and contracts the muscle.

  • Myofibrils: rod-like structures inside each fiber.
  • Sarcomere: the repeating unit of a myofibril and the unit of contraction.
  • A band: contains thick myosin filaments.
  • I band: contains thin actin filaments.
  • Z lines: separate the sarcomeres.

lessons.title: Muscle Contraction — Antagonistic Action, Calcium and the Cross-Bridge Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
Antagonistic muscles

Muscles work in antagonistic pairs, so when one muscle, the agonist, contracts to produce a movement, the opposite antagonist muscle relaxes. An antagonist muscle is relaxed while the muscle opposite to it is contracted. For example, during flexion of the forearm the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes.

Why calcium is essential for cross bridge formation

When a muscle is stimulated, calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the muscle fiber. Calcium binds with troponin, which moves tropomyosin away from the active sites on actin, so the myosin heads can attach to actin and form cross bridges. Without calcium the active sites remain covered and contraction cannot begin.

How nervous coordination regulates muscle contraction

A motor neuron carries the impulse to the muscle, and at the neuromuscular junction it releases acetylcholine, which generates an action potential in the muscle fiber membrane. This action potential spreads through the T-tubules and causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium ions, which trigger cross bridge formation and contraction. When the nerve impulse stops, calcium is pumped back and the muscle relaxes, so the nervous system controls both the start and the strength of contraction.

  • Motor neuron: carries the impulse to the muscle.
  • Acetylcholine: released at the neuromuscular junction; generates an action potential in the muscle fiber membrane.
  • T-tubules: spread the action potential through the fiber.
  • Sarcoplasmic reticulum: releases calcium ions, which trigger cross bridge formation and contraction.

Cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction

In the cross-bridge cycle, calcium first exposes the active sites on actin, and the energized myosin head, carrying ADP and phosphate, attaches to actin to form a cross bridge. The myosin head then bends in a power stroke, pulling the actin filament towards the center of the sarcomere and releasing ADP and phosphate. A new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head, which detaches it from actin, and breakdown of this ATP re-energizes the head so the cycle can repeat. Repeated cycles slide the actin filaments over myosin and shorten the sarcomere, producing contraction.

  • Cross bridge formation: the energized myosin head, carrying ADP and phosphate, attaches to actin.
  • Power stroke: the myosin head bends, pulling the actin filament towards the center of the sarcomere and releasing ADP and phosphate.
  • Detachment: a new ATP molecule binds to the myosin head and detaches it from actin.
  • Re-energizing: breakdown of this ATP re-energizes the head so the cycle can repeat.

lessons.title: The Neuron — Structure, Types and Function
lessons.notes_html:
Components of the nervous system

The nervous system makes rapid communication and coordination in the body possible. Neurons generate and conduct nerve impulses, so sensory neurons carry information from receptors to the CNS, interneurons integrate it, and motor neurons carry commands to effectors.

Structure of a neuron

A neuron consists of three main parts: the cell body (soma), the dendrites and the axon.

  • Cell body (soma): contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and controls the metabolic activities of the cell.
  • Dendrites: short branched processes that receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body.
  • Axon: a long fiber that carries impulses away from the cell body to other neurons, muscles or glands, often covered by a myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier.

Types of neurons by function

  • Sensory neurons: carry information from receptors to the CNS.
  • Interneurons: integrate information within the CNS.
  • Motor neurons: carry commands to effectors.

Most neurons of the brain are interneurons, which lie entirely within the central nervous system and connect sensory and motor neurons. They are responsible for integration, processing and decision making in the brain and spinal cord.

Why interneurons are called association neurons

Interneurons lie between sensory and motor neurons within the central nervous system and connect, or associate, them with each other. They receive information from sensory neurons, process and integrate it, and pass suitable commands to motor neurons. Because of this associating and connecting role, they are called association neurons.

How the nervous system alters target cells

A nervous system can alter activities in its target cells in muscles and glands because the target cells have receptor proteins for the signals released by the nervous system. Neurons release neurotransmitters at their endings, and only those muscle or gland cells that carry matching receptor proteins respond to them. This receptor specificity allows the nervous system to alter the activity of selected target cells.

Sensory neuronsCarry information from receptors to the CNS
InterneuronsIntegration, processing and decision making in the brain and spinal cord; connect sensory and motor neurons
Motor neuronsCarry commands to effectors

lessons.title: Nerve Impulse — Polarized Membrane, Threshold and Action Potential
lessons.notes_html:
Why the neurolemma is polarized

At rest, the inside of the neuron contains more potassium ions and negatively charged proteins, while the outside has more sodium ions, and the sodium-potassium pump keeps pumping Na+ out and K+ in. As a result the inner surface of the neurolemma (axon membrane) is negative and the outer surface is positive, with a resting potential of about -70 mV. This separation of charge across the membrane is why the neurolemma is called polarized.

Hyperpolarization

For a neuron with an initial membrane potential at -70mv, an increase in the movement of potassium ions out of that neuron's cytoplasm would result in hyperpolarization of the neuron. Potassium ions carry positive charge, so their increased movement out of the cell makes the inside even more negative than -70 mV. This increase in negativity is called hyperpolarization, and it makes the neuron less likely to fire.

Threshold potential

Threshold potential is the minimum level of depolarization, about -55 mV, which a stimulus must produce in the neuron membrane for an action potential to be generated. A stimulus weaker than threshold produces no impulse, while any stimulus reaching threshold produces a full action potential. It therefore follows the all-or-none principle.

  • Resting potential: about -70 mV.
  • Threshold potential: about -55 mV.
  • All-or-none principle: a stimulus weaker than threshold produces no impulse, while any stimulus reaching threshold produces a full action potential.

Mechanism of action potential

The action potential is a rapid, temporary reversal of membrane potential produced when a stimulus reaches threshold. First, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na+ rushes into the axon, so the inside becomes positive (up to about +40 mV); this is depolarization. Then sodium channels close and potassium channels open, K+ moves out, and the membrane returns to its negative resting value; this is repolarization, sometimes followed by brief hyperpolarization. The sodium-potassium pump then restores the original ion distribution, and the action potential travels along the axon as each neighboring region is depolarized in turn.

StageWhat happens

RepolarizationSodium channels close and potassium channels open, K+ moves out, and the membrane returns to its negative resting value, sometimes followed by brief hyperpolarization

lessons.title: Conduction in Myelinated Axons and Synaptic Transmission
lessons.notes_html:
Why impulses move faster in myelinated neurons

Action potentials move along axons more rapidly in myelinated than in non-myelinated axons. In myelinated neurons the myelin sheath insulates the axon, and the action potential is generated only at the exposed nodes of Ranvier. The impulse therefore jumps rapidly from node to node instead of traveling continuously along the whole membrane. Larger diameter also increases speed.

Saltatory conduction

Saltatory conduction is the jumping movement of the nerve impulse from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon. The action potential is regenerated only at the nodes, while the myelinated parts are insulated. This makes conduction fast and also saves energy for the neuron. This saltatory conduction makes conduction many times faster than in non-myelinated neurons.

The synapse — presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes

The surface on a neuron that discharges vesicles is the presynaptic membrane. The presynaptic membrane of the axon terminal discharges synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. The postsynaptic membrane only receives the transmitter through its receptors.

Neurotransmitter receptors are located on the postsynaptic membrane, facing the synaptic cleft. When transmitter released from the presynaptic side binds to them, ion channels open and a postsynaptic potential is produced.

  • Presynaptic membrane: discharges synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.
  • Postsynaptic membrane: receives the transmitter through its receptors, which are located on it.

Electrical and chemical synapse

The impulse passes directly through gap junctions between cells, so transmission is very fast and can be two-wayA neurotransmitter carries the signal across the synaptic cleft, so transmission is slower and one-way

Excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters

An inhibitory postsynaptic potential is produced when the membrane becomes more permeable to potassium ions (and chloride ions), so positive charge leaves the cell and the inside becomes more negative. This hyperpolarization moves the membrane away from threshold and inhibits firing. An inhibitory postsynaptic potential occurs in a membrane made more permeable to potassium ions.

  • Excitatory neurotransmitters: such as acetylcholine and glutamate depolarize the postsynaptic membrane and promote firing.
  • Inhibitory neurotransmitters: such as GABA hyperpolarize it and prevent firing.
  • GABA: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain, reducing the activity of neurons and preventing over-excitation. It is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain.
  • Acetylcholine and epinephrine: mainly act as excitatory transmitters at most of their sites.
  • Endorphins: natural pain-relieving chemicals produced by the brain that block pain pathways and produce a feeling of well-being.

lessons.notes_html:
Protection and divisions of the brain

The human brain is protected inside the skull by the bony cranium, three meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, and is divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

Forebrain

The forebrain includes the cerebrum, the largest part, whose cerebral cortex controls intelligence, memory, voluntary actions and sensations, and the diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus), which relays sensory information and regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature and endocrine activity.

  • Cerebrum: the largest part of the forebrain; its cerebral cortex controls intelligence, memory, voluntary actions and sensations.
  • Diencephalon: part of the forebrain; the thalamus and hypothalamus relay sensory information and regulate hunger, thirst, body temperature and endocrine activity.

Midbrain

The small midbrain acts mainly as a relay center for visual and auditory information. The midbrain forms the upper part of the brainstem.

Hindbrain

The hindbrain consists of the cerebellum, which coordinates movement and balance, and the pons and medulla, which control vital involuntary functions such as breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.

  • Cerebellum: part of the hindbrain, not of the midbrain; it coordinates movement and balance.
  • Pons and medulla: part of the hindbrain; they control vital involuntary functions such as breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.

lessons.title: Sensory Receptors and the Reflex Arc
lessons.notes_html:
Why receptors are called transducers

A transducer is a device that converts one form of energy into another form. Sensory receptors convert the energy of a stimulus, such as light, sound, pressure or heat, into electrical energy in the form of nerve impulses. Because of this conversion of stimulus energy into action potentials, receptors are called biological transducers.

Sensory receptors and their working

Sensory receptors are specialized cells or neuron endings that detect a specific stimulus and convert it into nerve impulses. When a stimulus of sufficient strength acts on a receptor, it produces a generator potential, and if this reaches threshold, action potentials are fired whose frequency reflects the strength of the stimulus. These impulses travel through sensory neurons to the CNS, where the sensation is perceived and a suitable response is organized.

Types of receptors

They are classified by the stimulus they detect.

  • Mechanoreceptors: for touch, pressure and sound; mechanoreceptors detect sound vibrations.
  • Chemoreceptors: for taste, smell and blood chemicals; chemoreceptors detect solute concentration.
  • Thermoreceptors: for temperature; thermoreceptors detect heat.
  • Photoreceptors: (rods and cones) for light.
  • Nociceptors: for pain; pain receptors that respond to damaging stimuli and produce the sensation of pain.
  • Pacinian corpuscles: pressure receptors deep in the skin and tissues that detect deep pressure and vibrations.

Pain receptors (nociceptors) respond to damaging mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli, not to electricity as their specific energy.

Reflex arc

A reflex arc is the pathway of a reflex action: receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron in the CNS, motor neuron and effector.

  • Receptor: detects the stimulus.
  • Sensory neuron: carries the impulse from the receptor.
  • Interneuron in the CNS: connects the sensory and motor neurons.
  • Motor neuron: carries the command from the CNS.
  • Effector: carries out the response.

lessons.title: Hormones and Their Mode of Action
lessons.notes_html:
Hormones — the chemical messengers

Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood, which regulate the activity of specific target organs. Hormones are chemical substances produced by endocrine glands in very small amounts and carried by the blood to distant target organs. Like messengers, they carry information and instructions from one part of the body to another and tell the target cells to start, stop or adjust a particular activity. For this reason they are called chemical messengers.

Hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate activities within the same organism, being carried by the blood from endocrine glands to their target organs. Communication between different organisms is done by pheromones, not by hormones.

  • Produced by: endocrine glands.
  • Chemical nature: modified amino acids, peptides or steroid molecules.
  • Carried by: the circulatory system.
  • Action: within the same organism, on specific target organs.

Hormones formed from tyrosine

Epinephrine and the other catecholamines of the adrenal medulla are derived from the amino acid tyrosine, and thyroxine of the thyroid gland is also formed from tyrosine units. Hence epinephrine, catecholamines and thyroxin all share tyrosine as their starting material.

Definition of a hormone

A hormone is a chemical messenger produced by an endocrine gland, released directly into the blood in small quantity, and carried to a specific target organ where it regulates its activity. In both modes of action the hormone is recognized only by cells carrying its specific receptor, which is why its action remains target-specific.

Action of hydrophilic hormones

Hydrophilic (water-soluble) hormones such as peptides and catecholamines cannot pass through the lipid plasma membrane of the target cell. They therefore bind to receptors on the cell surface, and the message is carried inside the cell by a second messenger such as cyclic AMP, which activates enzymes and produces the response. The hormone itself acts as the first messenger outside the cell.

Hydrophilic hormones cannot cross the cell membrane, so they bind to surface receptors and act through a second messenger such as cyclic AMP, which activates enzymes inside the cell and produces a rapid response.

Why hydrophilic hormones need secondary messengers

Hydrophilic hormones need secondary messengers because they cannot pass through the lipid plasma membrane of the target cell. They bind to receptors on the cell surface, and the message is carried inside the cell by a second messenger such as cyclic AMP, which activates enzymes and produces the response.

Action of lipophilic hormones

Lipophilic hormones such as steroids and thyroxine pass through the membrane, bind to receptors inside the cell or nucleus, and switch on specific genes, producing a slower but longer-lasting response through new protein synthesis.

Thyroid and steroid hormones are lipid soluble, so they pass through the plasma membrane and bind to receptors inside the cell, in the cytoplasm or nucleus. The hormone-receptor complex then switches specific genes on or off, changing protein synthesis in the target cell.

lessons.notes_html:
The pituitary gland

The pituitary gland is a pea-sized master gland hanging from the hypothalamus below the brain, and it has two main lobes. Because it controls so many other glands through its tropic hormones, the pituitary is called the master endocrine gland.

  • Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis): glandular in origin.
  • Posterior lobe (neurohypophysis): nervous in origin.

Anterior pituitary hormones

The anterior pituitary secretes six main hormones: growth hormone (GH or somatotropin) for body growth, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) for the thyroid, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) for the adrenal cortex, follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) for the gonads, and prolactin for milk production in the mammary glands. Most of these, except GH and prolactin, are tropic hormones that control other endocrine glands.

The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) is glandular and secretes growth hormone, prolactin and the tropic hormones TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH, which control growth, milk production and the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads respectively.

Oxytocin and ADH (vasopressin) are actually synthesized by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus. They are then transported down the axons and stored in the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary), from where they are released into the blood.

lessons.notes_html:
Pancreas — a mixed gland

The pancreas works in both ways, so it is a mixed gland. Its acinar cells act as an exocrine part and pour pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes through a duct into the duodenum. Its islets of Langerhans act as the endocrine part and release hormones directly into the blood: insulin from beta cells, glucagon from alpha cells and somatostatin from delta cells.

Insulin and glucagon

InsulinGlucagon
From beta cells of the pancreasFrom alpha cells of the pancreas
Lowers blood glucose by promoting its uptake and glycogen formationRaises blood glucose by breaking down glycogen in the liver

Adrenal glands — position

There are two adrenal (suprarenal) glands, one sitting like a cap on top of each kidney. Each gland has an outer cortex and an inner medulla with different functions.

Adrenal cortex and corticosteroids

All hormones of the adrenal cortex are chemically steroids and are synthesized from cholesterol. Because they are steroid hormones produced by the cortex, they are collectively called corticosteroids. They include glucocorticoids (e.g. cortisol), mineralocorticoids (e.g. aldosterone) and small amounts of sex steroids.

The cortex secretes corticosteroids - glucocorticoids such as cortisol, which regulate carbohydrate metabolism and stress responses, mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, which regulate salt, water and blood pressure, and small amounts of sex hormones.

The adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones, namely glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids, all made from cholesterol. Removal of the cortex would therefore directly abolish this steroid group, while peptide and amino-acid-derived hormones are made elsewhere.

Glucocorticoids and stress

Glucocorticoids such as cortisol are secreted by the adrenal cortex during stress and promote gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from amino acids and other non-carbohydrate substrates. This raises blood glucose to meet the increased energy demand of the stress condition. Glucocorticoids are secreted by the adrenal gland in response to stress and promote the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate substrates.

Adrenal medulla

The medulla secretes the catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine, which prepare the body for emergency by increasing heartbeat, blood pressure and blood glucose. Together the two parts help the body handle stress and maintain salt, water and energy balance.

Besides the main glands, several other tissues produce hormones with important functions.

lessons.title: Stimuli, Reflexes and Innate Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
Stimuli and responses

A stimulus is any detectable change, physical or chemical, in the internal or external environment of an organism, such as light, heat, sound, touch or a chemical. Organisms detect stimuli through receptors and respond through nerve impulses, hormones and muscles or glands. The response may be movement toward or away from the stimulus, a reflex, or a change in internal activity that helps survival.

Reflexes

A reflex is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought and follows a fixed reflex arc of receptor, sensory neuron, central nervous system, motor neuron and effector.

  • Knee-jerk reflex: an example of a reflex in vertebrates.
  • Blinking: blinking of the eye when an object approaches is an example of a reflex in vertebrates.
  • Withdrawal of the hand: withdrawal of the hand from a hot object is an example of a reflex in vertebrates.
  • Salivation: salivation at the sight or smell of food is another common example.

Heredity and behaviour

Heredity provides the basic pattern of behaviour through genes, so innate behaviours such as reflexes, instincts and fixed action patterns are inherited and appear without learning. Genes also set the limits within which learning can modify behaviour. Thus behaviour is a product of both inherited tendencies and experience, and closely related animals show similar behaviour because they share similar genes.

Innate behaviour and learning behaviour

Innate behaviour is inborn and inherited, is present at birth, needs no experience or practice, and is similar in all members of a species, for example reflexes and nest building. Learning behaviour is acquired during life through experience and practice, differs from individual to individual, and can be changed or improved. Innate behaviour is controlled mainly by genes, while learned behaviour depends on the nervous system and memory.

FeatureInnate behaviourLearning behaviour

VariationSimilar in all members of a speciesDiffers from individual to individual, and can be changed or improved

Innate behaviour in terms of reflexes in vertebrates and invertebrates

Innate behaviour is the inherited behaviour performed by an organism from birth in response to a stimulus without prior experience or learning. Its simplest form is the reflex, a rapid automatic response through a reflex arc, such as the knee-jerk, blinking and hand-withdrawal reflexes in vertebrates and the withdrawal of a snail or earthworm on touch in invertebrates. In invertebrates, innate behaviour also appears as kinesis and taxis, for example woodlice moving faster in dry conditions until they reach moisture. In vertebrates, more complex innate patterns develop into instincts and fixed action patterns, but all are built on inherited nervous pathways and need no practice.

Instinctive behaviour

Migration of salmon, dances of bees and nest building by birds are classic inborn instinctive patterns performed without learning.

  • Migration of Salmon Fish: salmon migrate from the sea back to the river of their birth to breed without ever being taught the route. This inborn, inherited pattern is an example of instinctive behaviour.
  • Dances of bees: a classic inborn instinctive pattern performed without learning.
  • Nest building by birds: a classic inborn instinctive pattern performed without learning.

Construction of an intricate web by a spider as instinct behaviour

Web building by a spider is a classic example of instinct, because a young spider raised in isolation builds a perfect web of its species without ever seeing one or being taught. The spider first lays a bridge thread across a gap, then builds a frame and radial threads from a central hub. It then lays a temporary spiral and replaces it with a sticky capture spiral, testing tension and spacing as it works. The whole sequence is a fixed, inherited pattern released by internal readiness and simple stimuli, and it serves the adaptive purpose of catching prey.

lessons.title: Learned Behaviour — Habituation, Imprinting, Insight and Operant Learning
lessons.notes_html:
Habituation — the simplest form of learning

Habituation is the decrease in response to repeated or continuous stimulation. When a stimulus is repeated again and again without any reward or harm, the animal gradually stops responding to it. This simplest form of learning is called habituation.

Habituation is the simplest form of learning in which an animal learns to ignore a repeated stimulus that brings neither benefit nor harm. It saves the animal from wasting energy on useless responses.

  • Repeated stimulus: a repeated, irrelevant stimulus that brings neither benefit nor harm is gradually ignored.
  • Effect: the animal learns not to respond or to ignore the stimulus, saving energy that would be wasted on useless responses.

Imprinting

Imprinting is a rapid type of learning that occurs during a short sensitive period early in life, in which a young animal fixes its attention on the first moving object it sees and thereafter follows it. Konrad Lorenz showed that newly hatched ducks and goslings follow the first moving object, normally their mother, but they can even be imprinted on a human or an object if that is what they first encounter.

How imprinting is adaptive

Imprinting is adaptive because the young stay close to the mother, who protects, warms and guides them to food, greatly increasing their chances of survival.

Insight learning

In the 1920s Wolfgang Kohler experimented on chimpanzees and showed insight learning. The chimpanzees suddenly solved problems, for example by joining sticks or piling boxes to reach bananas, without gradual trial and error.

Operant learning

B. F. Skinner used the Skinner box to study operant learning in rats and pigeons. The animal learned to press a lever to obtain food as a reward, so its behaviour was shaped by its consequences. The Skinner box was used for operant learning.

lessons.title: Taxes, Kinesis and Biological Rhythms
lessons.notes_html:
Taxis

Taxis is a directional movement of a whole organism toward or away from a particular stimulus such as light, heat or a chemical. Taxis is a directed movement in which the whole organism moves toward a stimulus (positive taxis) or away from it (negative taxis). In kinesis, by contrast, the response is not directed toward or away from the stimulus.

  • Positive taxis: movement toward the stimulus, for example moths flying toward light (positive phototaxis) and a sperm moving toward chemicals from the egg (positive chemotaxis).
  • Negative taxis: movement away from the stimulus, for example a cockroach running away from light and an earthworm moving away from strong light or dryness.
TypeDirectionExamples
Positive taxisToward the stimulusMoths flying toward light (positive phototaxis); a sperm moving toward chemicals from the egg (positive chemotaxis)
Negative taxisAway from the stimulusA cockroach running away from light; an earthworm moving away from strong light or dryness

Kinesis and other simple behaviour patterns

In kinesis, the response is not directed toward or away from the stimulus. In invertebrates, innate behaviour appears as kinesis and taxis, for example woodlice moving faster in dry conditions until they reach moisture.

Biological rhythms and the biological clock

The cyclic physiological patterns of activities in an organism that are in response to periodic environmental changes are biological rhythms. Regular cycles of activity controlled by an internal biological clock in response to periodic changes such as day and night are called biological rhythms, and the daily ones are circadian rhythms.

Biological rhythms are the cyclic physiological patterns of activity in an organism that occur in response to periodic environmental changes and are controlled by an internal biological clock.

Importance of biological rhythms to man

In man biological rhythms regulate the sleep-wake cycle, body temperature, hormone secretion and alertness in a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm. Disturbance of these rhythms, for example by night shifts or jet lag, causes tiredness and poor performance, so they are important for health and normal daily life.

  • Body temperature: regulated in a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm.
  • Hormone secretion: regulated in a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm.
  • Alertness: regulated in a roughly 24-hour circadian rhythm.

lessons.title: Social Behaviour — Agonistic Behaviour, Territories and Dominance Hierarchies
lessons.notes_html:
Social behaviour

Agonistic behaviour is a type of social behaviour. Agonistic behaviour includes aggression, threat displays, submission and fighting between members of the same species. Because it occurs during social interactions over food, mates or territory, it is a type of social behaviour.

Territorial behaviour in Gorillas is classified as agonistic social behaviour shown in interaction with other members of the group.

Agonistic behaviour

Agonistic behaviour is the aggressive and submissive behaviour shown when animals of the same species compete for food, mates, shelter or territory; it includes threat displays, posturing, vocalizations, chasing and sometimes fighting.

  • Threat displays: part of agonistic behaviour.
  • Posturing: part of agonistic behaviour.
  • Vocalizations: part of agonistic behaviour.
  • Chasing: part of agonistic behaviour.
  • Fighting: sometimes part of agonistic behaviour.
  • Submission: agonistic behaviour includes aggression, threat displays, submission and fighting between members of the same species.

Territories and the maintenance of social order

By defending a territory, an animal secures enough food and a breeding place, and rivals are kept out mostly by displays rather than injurious fights. Within a group, contests establish a dominance hierarchy or pecking order in which higher-ranking animals get first access to resources and lower-ranking ones submit. In this way agonistic behaviour maintains social order, reduces repeated fighting and stabilizes group life.

FeatureRole in social order
Territory defenceSecures enough food and a breeding place; rivals are kept out mostly by displays rather than injurious fights
Dominance hierarchy / pecking orderHigher-ranking animals get first access to resources and lower-ranking ones submit
Overall effectMaintains social order, reduces repeated fighting and stabilizes group life

How old world monkeys defend their territory

Old world monkeys live in troops and defend their home territory by group displays and aggression against intruding troops. Dominant males give loud calls, show threatening gestures and expose their large canine teeth, and may chase or fight intruders. Such agonistic displays usually settle the dispute without serious injury and keep other troops away from their food and resting sites.

lessons.notes_html:
Social organisation in honey bees

In a honey bee colony the workers are sterile females. The workers are females that cannot reproduce. They perform all the colony work such as collecting food, cleaning, feeding larvae and defending the hive, while the queen is the fertile female.

  • Workers: sterile females that cannot reproduce; they perform all the colony work such as collecting food, cleaning, feeding larvae and defending the hive.
  • Queen: the fertile female in a honey bee colony.
MemberFertilityRole
Workers (honey bee)Sterile femalesCollecting food, cleaning, feeding larvae and defending the hive
QueenFertile femaleThe fertile female of the colony

How bees communicate about food sources

Honey bees communicate the distance and direction of a food source by performing dances on the comb, as described by Karl von Frisch. A round dance shows that food is near the hive, while a waggle dance, performed in a figure-of-eight with a waggling run, shows a distant source. The angle of the waggle run to the vertical indicates direction with respect to the sun, and the duration of waggling indicates distance.

  • Round dance: shows that food is near the hive.
  • Waggle dance: performed in a figure-of-eight with a waggling run; shows a distant source.
  • Direction: the angle of the waggle run to the vertical indicates direction with respect to the sun.
  • Distance: the duration of waggling indicates distance.

Waggle danceA distant source — performed in a figure-of-eight with a waggling run

Communication and group life

Communication about food sources by dances on the comb allows honey bees to share the distance and direction of a food source with other members of the colony. This communication, together with the division of work between the sterile female workers and the fertile queen, is part of the social organisation of the honey bee colony.

lessons.notes_html:
Male reproductive system

The male reproductive system consists of the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, accessory glands and penis.

  • Testes: held in the scrotum; they contain seminiferous tubules where sperm are produced and cells that secrete testosterone.
  • Epididymis: sperm mature and are stored in the coiled epididymis.
  • Vas deferens: sperm pass through the vas deferens to the urethra.
  • Accessory glands: the seminal vesicles, prostate gland and Cowper glands add fluids that nourish and protect sperm and form semen.
  • Penis: the copulatory organ that delivers semen into the female reproductive tract during intercourse.

Scrotum and temperature

The scrotum is the sac of skin that holds and protects the testes outside the body cavity. It keeps them about 2-3 degrees Celsius below normal body temperature, which is necessary for normal sperm production.

Why the testes descend before birth

The testes develop inside the abdomen of the foetus but descend into the scrotum before birth because sperm production requires a temperature about 2-3 degrees Celsius lower than the internal body temperature. Inside the abdomen the heat would damage the sperm-forming cells and cause sterility. Descent into the cooler scrotum therefore ensures normal spermatogenesis after puberty.

Urethra as the urinogenital duct

In the male, the urethra is a common passage for both urine and semen. Urine from the bladder and semen from the vas deferens both leave the body through it, though never at the same time. Because it serves both the urinary and the genital systems, it is called the urinogenital duct.

Female reproductive system

The female reproductive system consists of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina.

  • Ovaries: produce eggs and the hormones estrogen and progesterone, and release one egg each month at ovulation.
  • Fallopian tubes: the fallopian tubes (oviducts) carry the egg toward the uterus and are the usual site of fertilization.
  • Uterus: a muscular organ whose lining, the endometrium, receives the implanted embryo and nourishes the developing foetus during pregnancy.
  • Cervix: the narrow lower end of the uterus opening into the vagina.
  • Vagina: receives sperm during intercourse and forms the birth canal during childbirth.

Ovarian cycle and the mature follicle

During the ovarian cycle a primary follicle develops into a secondary follicle and then into the mature follicle. This mature follicle is called both the Graafian follicle and the vesicular follicle, so both names are correct. The ovarian cycle includes changes in ovarian follicles to secondary follicle and finally to Graafian follicle.

lessons.notes_html:
Phases of the menstrual cycle

The menstrual cycle of about 28 days has three main phases.

  • Menstrual phase (days 1-5): the thickened endometrium breaks down and is shed with blood through the vagina because no pregnancy has occurred.
  • Proliferative or follicular phase (days 6-14): FSH develops an ovarian follicle, and estrogen from the follicle repairs and thickens the endometrium, ending with ovulation around day 14.
  • Secretory or luteal phase (days 15-28): the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which makes the endometrium thick, vascular and secretory for possible implantation; if fertilization fails, hormone levels fall and the cycle repeats.

Why the inner uterine wall thickens in the secretory phase

During the secretory phase, progesterone from the corpus luteum makes the inner uterine wall (endometrium) thicken, become rich in blood vessels and glands that secrete nutrients. This prepares a soft, nourishing bed in which a fertilized egg can implant and grow. If fertilization does not occur, progesterone falls and this thickened lining is shed during menstruation.

Hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle

The menstrual cycle is regulated by FSH and LH from the pituitary together with estrogen and progesterone from the ovary. Androgens are male hormones and do not primarily regulate the female menstrual cycle.

  • Estrogen: under the influence of FSH the growing Graafian follicle secretes estrogen. Estrogen causes growth and repair of the uterine lining during the first half of the menstrual cycle.
  • Progesterone: estrogen and progesterone are the two key ovarian hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle, controlling follicle growth, ovulation and preparation of the uterus.
  • Testosterone: the main male hormone and is not a key regulator of the cycle.
HormoneRole in the cycle
FSHDevelops an ovarian follicle; induces the Graafian follicle to produce estrogen
LHRegulates the cycle together with FSH
EstrogenGrowth and repair of the uterine lining during the first half of the cycle
ProgesteroneMakes the endometrium thick, vascular and secretory in the secretory phase

Female hormonal system

The female hormonal system is considered better, or more finely regulated, because it works in a precise cyclic manner with feedback control between the pituitary and the ovaries. Estrogen and progesterone rise and fall in a coordinated sequence that controls follicle growth, ovulation, preparation of the uterus and, if pregnancy occurs, its maintenance. This regular hormonal cycle prepares the body every month for a possible pregnancy, a level of cyclic coordination not found in the male.

Causes of infertility

  • Male infertility: low sperm count, poor sperm motility or abnormal sperm, blocked vas deferens, hormonal imbalance, undescended testes and infections.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) disturbs ovulation, endometriosis damages the reproductive organs, and blocked fallopian tubes prevent the egg and sperm from meeting. Any of these can cause female infertility.

In-vitro fertilization (IVF)

In IVF, eggs are fertilized by sperm outside the body in the laboratory and the resulting embryo is placed in the uterus. It is an assisted reproductive technique used to help couples who cannot conceive naturally, and it is a method used to treat infertility.

Miscarriage

A miscarriage is the natural, spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before the foetus can survive outside the uterus. In medical terms it is called spontaneous abortion, whereas induced abortion is a deliberate termination.

Sexually transmitted diseases

  • Syphilis: a sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, transmitted through sexual contact. It produces sores and rashes and, if untreated, can damage the heart and nervous system, but it can be cured with antibiotics.
  • Gonorrhea: a bacterial sexually transmitted disease caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Its symptoms include a burning sensation and pain during urination and a thick yellow-green discharge from the urethra or vagina. If untreated it can inflame the reproductive organs and cause infertility, and some infected persons, especially women, may show few early symptoms.

Fertilization, Cleavage and the Blastocyst
lessons.notes_html:
Fertilization and the zygote

Fertilization normally takes place in the upper part of the fallopian tube (oviduct), where the sperm meets the egg released at ovulation. The fertilized egg then travels to the uterus for implantation.

At fertilization the haploid nucleus of the sperm fuses with the haploid nucleus of the egg. The resulting zygote therefore contains a complete diploid set of DNA, half from the mother and half from the father, so the genetic material of a fertilized egg is a combination of both the mother's and father's DNA.

Stages of embryonic development

After fertilization, the stages of embryonic development are cleavage, implantation, gastrulation, and organogenesis. The zygote undergoes cleavage to form a blastocyst, which implants in the uterus. Gastrulation then forms the three germ layers, and organogenesis forms the organs from these layers.

Cleavage and the morula

After fertilization the zygote undergoes repeated mitotic divisions called cleavage, first forming a solid morula and then the blastula, which in mammals is called the blastocyst.

  • Morula: the early embryonic stage formed by cleavage of the zygote, consisting of a solid ball of small cells called blastomeres. Its surface looks like a mulberry fruit (Morula is the Latin name related to mulberry), so it is named morula. It later develops a cavity and changes into the blastula or blastocyst.

Meroblastic cleavage in birds and reptiles

In birds and reptiles the egg contains a very large amount of yolk, and cleavage furrows cannot pass through the dense yolk. Only the small disc of cytoplasm on top of the yolk, the blastodisc, divides. Because cleavage is partial and incomplete, involving only part of the egg, it is called meroblastic cleavage.

Blastula and blastocyst — segmentation cavity

Cleavage creates a fluid-filled space inside, the segmentation cavity or blastocoel, formed as the blastomeres separate and fluid accumulates. In the mammalian blastocyst the cells are arranged as an outer layer, the trophoblast, which will form the placenta and membranes, and an inner cell mass attached at one side, which will form the embryo.

  • Trophoblast: the outer layer of the blastocyst; it mainly contributes to the placenta and foetal membranes.
  • Inner cell mass: gives rise to the embryo proper.
  • Segmentation cavity: the fluid-filled space inside, also called the blastocoel; it allows cell movements and rearrangement during the next stage, gastrulation, and in mammals gives the blastocyst the form that implants in the uterine wall.

lessons.title: Implantation, Gastrulation and Embryonic Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Implantation and development in the uterus

Human embryonic development occurs in the uterus. After fertilization in the fallopian tube, the embryo implants in the wall of the uterus. It then develops there, nourished through the placenta, until birth.

The fertilized egg divides during its journey down the fallopian tube and forms a blastocyst. About six to seven days, roughly one week, after fertilization the blastocyst implants in the endometrium of the uterus.

Blastula and gastrula

StructureAn early stage consisting of a hollow ball of cells (blastoderm) around a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel or segmentation cavityThe later stage formed by gastrulation, in which cells migrate inward

Embryonic induction — how tissues influence other tissues

Embryonic tissues influence neighbouring tissues by the process of induction, in which one tissue releases chemical signals that direct adjacent cells to differentiate in a particular way. For example, the chordamesoderm induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate and neural tube. Such interactions, controlled by signal molecules and gene switching, coordinate the orderly development of organs.

Organizers and primary and secondary induction

An organizer is a group of embryonic cells that influences the development of surrounding tissues and organizes the body plan, such as the dorsal lip of the blastopore in amphibians described by Spemann.

  • Primary induction: the first inductive interaction, in which the chordamesoderm induces the ectoderm to form the nervous system during gastrulation.
  • Secondary induction: occurs later between tissues formed after gastrulation, for example the optic vesicle inducing the overlying ectoderm to form the lens of the eye.

lessons.title: Germ Layers, Differentiation and Organogenesis
lessons.notes_html:
Cell differentiation

The process of cell differentiation involves the specialization of cells for different functions. In differentiation, cells that have the same genes switch on different genes and become specialized in structure and function, for example into muscle, nerve or blood cells. This specialization builds the different tissues and organs of the body.

Organogenesis and the neural tube

During organogenesis the ectoderm folds to form the neural tube, which develops into the brain and spinal cord. This process, called neurulation, is one of the earliest events in organ formation. The formation of the neural tube occurs during organogenesis.

Tissues and organs formed from the three germ layers

  • Ectoderm: forms the epidermis of the skin with hair, nails and skin glands, the whole nervous system including brain and spinal cord, the sensory epithelia of the eye, ear and nose, the lens and retina, and the enamel of teeth.
  • Mesoderm: forms muscles, bones and cartilage, connective tissues, the heart and blood vessels, blood, kidneys and ureters, the reproductive organs, the dermis of skin and the lining of the body cavity.
  • Endoderm: forms the lining of the digestive tract and respiratory tract, and the glands derived from them including the liver, pancreas, thyroid and thymus, as well as the lining of the urinary bladder.
Germ layerTissues and organs formed
EctodermEpidermis of the skin with hair, nails and skin glands; whole nervous system including brain and spinal cord; sensory epithelia of the eye, ear and nose; lens and retina; enamel of teeth
MesodermMuscles, bones and cartilage; connective tissues; heart and blood vessels; blood; kidneys and ureters; reproductive organs; dermis of skin; lining of the body cavity
EndodermLining of the digestive tract and respiratory tract; glands derived from them including liver, pancreas, thyroid and thymus; lining of the urinary bladder

Role of the nucleus and cytoplasm in controlling development

Experiments show that both the nucleus and the cytoplasm control development. In nuclear transplantation experiments, for example Briggs and King transplanted a nucleus from an early frog embryo into an enucleated egg and a normal tadpole developed, proving the nucleus carries the complete genetic instructions for development. Gurdon later obtained adult frogs from nuclei of tadpole intestinal cells, showing that differentiated cells retain all genes.

On the other hand, the egg cytoplasm contains maternal determinants distributed unevenly, and experiments such as constricting a fertilized egg show that regions lacking certain cytoplasmic substances fail to form particular structures. Development is therefore controlled by the genes of the nucleus acting in response to signals and substances in the surrounding cytoplasm.

lessons.title: Foetal Development, the Placenta and the Trimesters
lessons.notes_html:
The placenta

The placenta transfers oxygen and nutrients from the mother to the embryo and removes carbon dioxide and other waste products from the foetal blood. It also secretes hormones, such as progesterone, that maintain pregnancy.

  • Providing oxygen and nutrients: the placenta is responsible for providing oxygen and nutrients to the developing embryo.
  • Removing waste products: the placenta is responsible for removing waste products from the developing embryo.
  • Producing hormones: the placenta is responsible for producing hormones that maintain the pregnancy.

Development in the first, second and third trimesters

  • First trimester (weeks 1-12): fertilization, cleavage, implantation and gastrulation occur, the three germ layers form, and organogenesis builds all major organs; the heart starts beating, limb buds appear and by the end the embryo is called a foetus.
  • Second trimester (weeks 13-26): the foetus grows rapidly, bones ossify, hair and facial features form, movements are felt by the mother and the sex can be identified, while the organs mature.
  • Third trimester (weeks 27-40): growth and weight gain are greatest, the lungs mature with surfactant production, the foetus turns head-down, and it becomes capable of independent life at birth.

Monozygotic twins

Monozygotic twins develop from a single fertilized egg that splits into two embryos early in development. Because both embryos come from the same zygote, they carry identical chromosomes, including the same sex chromosomes (both XX or both XY). They are therefore always of the same sex and are called identical twins.

Maternal derived abnormalities

Maternal factors can disturb embryonic development, showing that a healthy maternal environment is essential for normal development.

  • Rubella: Rubella (German measles) virus crossing the placenta in early pregnancy can cause deafness, cataracts and heart defects in the baby.
  • Abnormal neural tube: failure of the neural tube to close properly produces abnormalities such as spina bifida and anencephaly, commonly linked with deficiency of folic acid in the mother.
  • Thyroid gland: maternal thyroid disorders, especially iodine deficiency and hypothyroidism, impair the baby's brain and skeletal development and can cause cretinism.
  • Limb development: drugs and harmful substances taken by the mother, such as thalidomide, can disturb limb development and produce short or missing limbs.

lessons.title: Aging — Accumulation of Mutations and Decline in Function
lessons.notes_html:
Aging

Aging is characterized by the accumulation of genetic mutations. With advancing age, DNA damage and mutations accumulate in cells while repair becomes less efficient.

Causes and effects of aging

  • Accumulation of genetic mutations: DNA damage and mutations accumulate in cells with advancing age.
  • Breakdown of cellular processes: the accumulation contributes to the gradual breakdown of cellular processes.
  • Decline in tissue and organ function: the breakdown leads to the decline in tissue and organ function seen in aging, as repair becomes less efficient.

This gradual decline is the pattern seen in aging: mutations accumulate, repair becomes less efficient, cellular processes break down gradually, and tissue and organ function declines.
