lessons.title: Chromosomes — Structure and the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance
lessons.notes_html:
Chromosomal theory of inheritance

The chromosomal theory of inheritance was proposed by Sutton and Boveri in 1902. It states that genes are located on chromosomes and that chromosomes are the carriers of heredity from one generation to the next. The nucleus is the storehouse of this hereditary material.

Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri observed that chromosomes are distributed during meiosis and fertilization in the same pattern as Mendel's hereditary factors. This parallel behaviour led them to propose the theory.

Parallel behaviour of chromosomes and Mendel's factors

  • Occur in pairs: chromosomes and Mendel's factors both occur in pairs.
  • Segregation: both segregate during meiosis so that each gamete receives one member of each pair.
  • Restoration at fertilization: both are restored at fertilization when the sperm and egg nuclei fuse.
  • Equal contribution: both parents make an equal hereditary contribution through their gametes, each gamete carrying one copy of each homologous chromosome.

The behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis thus explains Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment. Each parent makes an equal chromosomal contribution to the offspring.

FeatureChromosomesMendel's factors
OccurrenceOccur in pairsOccur in pairs
During meiosisSegregate, one member to each gameteSegregate, one member to each gamete
At fertilizationPairs restored when sperm and egg nuclei fusePairs restored in the offspring

Chemical structure of a chromosome

A chromosome is made of chromatin, which chemically consists of DNA, histone and non-histone proteins, and a small amount of RNA.

  • DNA: about 40 percent of the chromosome; the hereditary material carrying the genes.
  • Protein: about 60 percent, mainly basic histones around which the DNA is wound to form nucleosomes.
  • RNA: present in a small amount.

At division the chromatin condenses into the short, thick chromosome. This packing allows the very long DNA molecule to fit inside the nucleus and to be distributed accurately to daughter cells.

Sister chromatids and the centromere

After replication, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere. These chromatids separate during cell division so that each daughter cell receives one copy. At division the condensed chromosome therefore shows two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, with telomeres at the ends.

Nucleosome and chromatin packing

A nucleosome is the basic unit of chromatin packing, formed by about two loops of duplex DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, a histone octamer. A chain of nucleosomes gives chromatin its beads-on-a-string appearance.

  • Histone octamer: a core of eight histone proteins.
  • DNA wrapping: about two loops of duplex DNA wrapped around the octamer.
  • Nucleosome: the complex of histone octamer and two loops of duplex DNA.

lessons.title: DNA Structure, Genes and Gene Expression
lessons.notes_html:
Gene, genome and locus

A gene is a specific length of DNA that carries the coded information for making one particular polypeptide chain. A small part of DNA which has information to synthesize a specific polypeptide chain is a gene.

  • Gene: a specific length of DNA carrying the coded information for one particular polypeptide chain.
  • Genome: the total DNA of the cell.
  • Locus: the position of a gene on a chromosome.

Why DNA is a negatively charged molecule

DNA is negatively charged because each nucleotide of its backbone contains a phosphate group, and phosphate groups carry a negative charge at normal cellular pH. With thousands of phosphate groups along its length, the whole DNA molecule has a strong overall negative charge. This charge helps DNA associate with positively charged histone proteins to form chromatin.

  • Phosphate groups: each nucleotide of the backbone contains a phosphate group carrying a negative charge at normal cellular pH.
  • Overall charge: thousands of phosphate groups give the whole molecule a strong overall negative charge.
  • Association with histones: the negative charge helps DNA associate with positively charged histone proteins to form chromatin.

Gene expression

Gene expression is the overall process by which the information stored in a gene is used to produce a functional product, usually a protein. It includes transcription of the gene into mRNA and translation of mRNA into a polypeptide.

Genes in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

Prokaryotic and eukaryotic genes differ in structure.

OrganisationOften grouped in operonsEach gene is usually transcribed separately
DNA form and locationSingle circular DNA molecule in the nucleoidLinear DNA packed with histones in a membrane-bound nucleus

lessons.title: Replication of DNA
lessons.notes_html:
Models of DNA replication

In the conservative model, the parental double helix was proposed to remain completely intact and an entirely new double helix to be made. Actual DNA replication was later proved by Meselson and Stahl to be semi-conservative, not conservative.

Why replication is semi-conservative

Replication is called semi-conservative because each daughter DNA molecule formed consists of one old (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand. In this way half of the original molecule is conserved in each new molecule. The Meselson and Stahl experiment with nitrogen isotopes proved this mode of replication.

Meselson and Stahl proved this mechanism by growing bacteria on heavy nitrogen (N-15) and then on light nitrogen (N-14) and finding DNA of intermediate density after one generation.

The semi-conservative process

In semi-conservative replication the two strands of the parental double helix separate, and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so each daughter molecule keeps one old strand and gains one new strand.

  • Unwinding: helicase unwinds the helix at the origin and a replication fork forms, with SSB proteins holding the strands apart.
  • Priming: primase lays a short RNA primer.
  • Strand building: DNA polymerase III adds complementary nucleotides continuously on the leading strand and in Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
  • Finishing: polymerase I and ligase remove primers and seal the joins.

Leading and lagging strands

Because DNA polymerase can synthesize DNA only in the 5' to 3' direction and the two template strands are antiparallel, the two new strands are made differently.

  • Leading strand: synthesized continuously in the 5' to 3' direction, in the same direction as the movement of the replication fork, from a single primer.
  • Lagging strand: synthesized discontinuously, away from the fork, as short Okazaki fragments that are later joined by DNA ligase.
FeatureLeading strandLagging strand
Direction of synthesis5' to 3', same direction as fork movement5' to 3', away from the fork
ContinuityContinuousDiscontinuous, in short Okazaki fragments
PrimerSingle primerPrimer for each fragment
JoiningNo fragments to joinFragments later joined by DNA ligase

Single-strand binding proteins

Single-strand binding proteins (SSB) attach to the separated single strands of DNA at the replication fork. They keep the strands apart, prevent them from re-joining and protect them from damage until new strands are synthesized. A protein which prevents the re-binding of complementary strands during replication at the fork is SSB.

Enzymes involved in replication

  • Helicase: unwinds and separates the two strands.
  • Primase: lays down a short RNA primer.
  • DNA polymerase III: builds the new DNA strand.
  • DNA polymerase I: removes the primer and fills the gap.
  • Ligase: joins the Okazaki fragments.
  • SSB proteins: keep the single strands separated.
  • Topoisomerase: relieves the twisting strain ahead of the fork.

mcqs.why: Because DNA polymerase synthesizes only in the 5' to 3' direction and the template strands are antiparallel, one strand is continuous and the other is made in fragments.

mcqs.why: The two strands of the parental double helix separate and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand, so each daughter keeps one old strand.

lessons.title: Transcription and mRNA Processing
lessons.notes_html:
Transcription

Transcription is the first step of gene expression, in which the information of one gene on DNA is copied into a complementary messenger RNA by the enzyme RNA polymerase.

  • Binding: the polymerase binds at the promoter and unwinds a short length of DNA.
  • Reading the template: the polymerase reads the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction.
  • Building mRNA: complementary RNA nucleotides are joined, with uracil in place of thymine, to build mRNA in the 5' to 3' direction.
  • Termination: transcription continues until a terminator sequence is reached, when the mRNA is released.

In eukaryotes the transcript is then capped, tailed and spliced before it leaves the nucleus for translation.

Introns are transcribed but not translated

Introns are transcribed, because RNA polymerase copies the whole gene, including both exons and introns, into the primary mRNA transcript. However, introns are not involved in translation, because they are cut out during splicing before the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus. Only the joined exons are read by the ribosome to make the protein.

  • Transcription: the whole gene, exons and introns, is copied into the primary transcript.
  • Splicing: introns are cut out before the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus.
  • Translation: only the joined exons are read by the ribosome.

Processing of mRNA before it leaves the nucleus

Before leaving the nucleus, eukaryotic mRNA is processed in three ways. This mature mRNA is stable, is protected from degradation, and can be translated in the cytoplasm. Only after this processing does the mRNA pass through the nuclear pores to the ribosomes.

  • 5' cap: a cap is added at the 5' end.
  • Poly-A tail: a poly-A tail is added at the 3' end.
  • Splicing: the introns are spliced out so that the exons join together.
ChangeWhere / what happens
CapAdded at the 5' end
Poly-A tailAdded at the 3' end
SplicingIntrons removed, exons joined together

lessons.title: Translation — tRNA and the Ribosome
lessons.notes_html:
Sites at the ribosome during translation

The large subunit of the ribosome has three sites for tRNA during translation. The ribosome moves along the mRNA codon by codon, linking amino acids into a chain at these sites.

  • A site: the aminoacyl site; receives the incoming tRNA carrying the next amino acid.
  • P site: the peptidyl site; holds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain.
  • E site: the exit site; where the empty tRNA leaves the ribosome.
SiteFull nameFunction
AAminoacyl siteReceives the incoming tRNA carrying the next amino acid
PPeptidyl siteHolds the tRNA carrying the growing polypeptide chain
EExit siteEmpty tRNA leaves the ribosome

Structure of tRNA

A tRNA molecule is folded into a clover-leaf shape with several important regions.

  • Amino acid attachment site: at the 3' end is the CCA end, which carries a specific amino acid.
  • Anticodon loop: at the opposite end; its three-base anticodon pairs with the complementary codon on mRNA.
  • D loop and T loop: help the molecule bind correctly to the ribosome and to its specific activating enzyme.

Function of tRNA

The tRNA delivers the correct amino acid to the growing chain at the ribosome. Its anticodon ensures pairing with the complementary codon on mRNA, its 3' CCA end carries the specific amino acid, and its D and T loops help it bind correctly to the ribosome and to its specific activating enzyme.

lessons.title: Genetic Code, Mutations and Gene Regulation
lessons.notes_html:
The genetic code

The genetic code is the set of rules by which triplet sequences of bases in DNA and mRNA specify the amino acids of a protein. It is the set of rules used to store the genetic information within DNA for particular protein synthesis.

  • Genetic code: the set of rules by which triplet sequences of bases in DNA and mRNA specify the amino acids of a protein.
  • Codon: a single triplet within this code.
  • Anticodon: the matching triplet on tRNA.

Mutation is not always harmful

Mutation is not always harmful.

  • Neutral mutations: many mutations are neutral because they occur in non-coding DNA or do not change the amino acid produced, so they have no visible effect.
  • Harmful mutations: some mutations are harmful and cause genetic disorders.
  • Beneficial mutations: a few are beneficial, giving the organism an advantage in survival and reproduction.

Such useful variations are the raw material of evolution and of plant and animal breeding.

Type of effectOutcome
NeutralOccurs in non-coding DNA or does not change the amino acid; no visible effect
HarmfulCauses genetic disorders
BeneficialGives an advantage in survival and reproduction; raw material of evolution and breeding

Gene regulation

Gene regulation is the turning ON and OFF of genes so that a cell makes only the proteins it needs, at the right time and in the right amount.

Gene regulation in prokaryotes

In prokaryotes regulation occurs mainly at transcription through operons, where a repressor protein blocks the operator to switch genes off, and removal of the repressor or binding of an activator switches them on, as in the lac operon.

  • Repressor: a protein that blocks the operator to switch genes off.
  • Switching on: removal of the repressor or binding of an activator switches genes on.
  • Example: the lac operon.

Gene regulation in eukaryotes

In eukaryotes regulation occurs at many levels: chromatin opening, control of transcription by regulatory proteins, mRNA processing, mRNA breakdown and control of translation. Such regulation allows cells with identical genes to differentiate into different types and to respond to changing conditions.

  • Chromatin opening: regulation at the level of chromatin.
  • Transcription control: control of transcription by regulatory proteins.
  • mRNA levels: mRNA processing and mRNA breakdown.
  • Translation control: control of translation.

mcqs.q: The genetic code is best defined as:
options: The position of a gene on a chromosome
The total DNA of the cell
The set of rules by which triplet sequences of bases specify the amino acids of a protein
mcqs.why: The genetic code is the set of rules by which triplet sequences of bases in DNA and mRNA specify the amino acids of a protein.

mcqs.q: A codon is:
options: A single triplet within the genetic code
The whole set of coding rules
A protein that blocks the operator
mcqs.why: A codon is a single triplet within the genetic code, while the anticodon is the matching triplet on tRNA.

mcqs.q: An anticodon is:
options: A sequence at the end of mRNA
A repressor protein in an operon
mcqs.why: An anticodon is the matching triplet on tRNA that pairs with a codon, as distinct from the codon itself within the genetic code.

mcqs.q: A mutation is neutral when it:
options: Occurs in non-coding DNA or does not change the amino acid produced
mcqs.why: Many mutations are neutral because they occur in non-coding DNA or do not change the amino acid produced, so they have no visible effect.

mcqs.q: Beneficial mutations are important because they:
options: Give the organism an advantage in survival and reproduction and are the raw material of evolution
mcqs.why: A few mutations are beneficial, giving an advantage in survival and reproduction, and such useful variations are the raw material of evolution and breeding.

mcqs.q: Harmful mutations are those that:
mcqs.why: Some mutations are harmful and cause genetic disorders, while many others are neutral and a few are beneficial, so mutation is not always harmful.

mcqs.q: Gene regulation is:
options: The copying of DNA before division
The turning ON and OFF of genes so a cell makes only the proteins it needs, at the right time and amount
mcqs.why: Gene regulation is the turning ON and OFF of genes so that a cell makes only the proteins it needs, at the right time and in the right amount.

mcqs.q: In prokaryotes, a repressor protein switches genes off by:
options: Blocking the operator in an operon
mcqs.why: In prokaryotes regulation occurs mainly at transcription through operons, where a repressor protein blocks the operator to switch genes off, as in the lac operon.

mcqs.q: Genes in a prokaryotic operon are switched on when:
options: The repressor is removed or an activator binds
Introns are spliced out in the nucleus
mcqs.why: Removal of the repressor or binding of an activator switches operon genes on, as in the lac operon example of prokaryotic regulation.

mcqs.q: In eukaryotes, gene regulation occurs at many levels including:
options: Only the operator of an operon
Only the joining of DNA fragments
Chromatin opening, control of transcription, mRNA processing and breakdown, and control of translation
Only the formation of the replication fork
mcqs.why: Eukaryotic regulation occurs at many levels: chromatin opening, transcription control by regulatory proteins, mRNA processing, mRNA breakdown and control of translation.

lessons.title: Mendel's Laws — Monohybrid, Dihybrid, Segregation and Independent Assortment
lessons.notes_html:
Genetics, genes and alleles

Genetics is the branch of biology that studies heredity and variation. Organisms with the same genotype can look different when they grow under different conditions of food, light, temperature or water. Such variation is environmental and is not inherited.

  • Gene: a specific part of DNA that controls one hereditary character.
  • Allele: an alternative form of a gene present at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
  • Genotype and environment: the genotype sets the hereditary characters, while different environments can produce phenotypic variation among organisms of the same genotype.

Monohybrid and dihybrid crosses

CrossWhat it studies
Monohybrid crossOne contrasting trait at a time
Dihybrid crossTwo traits at the same time

Law of segregation — purity of gametes

According to the law of segregation, the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one allele and remains pure for that character. A gamete never carries both alleles together, therefore this law is called the law of purity of gametes.

Dihybrid cross — inheritance of two traits

Inheritance of two traits is studied by a dihybrid cross, for example a cross between pea plants with round yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled green seeds (rryy). All F1 plants are heterozygous (RrYy) with round yellow seeds, showing that round and yellow are dominant.

Each gene pair segregates and assorts independently, producing four types of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) from each parent. The appearance of new combinations, round green and wrinkled yellow, proves the law of independent assortment.

F2 phenotypeRatio
Round yellow9
Round green3
Wrinkled yellow3
Wrinkled green1

On self-crossing, F1 gives F2 in the ratio 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.

mcqs.q: What is genetics?
options: The branch of biology that studies heredity and variation
The study of fossils and extinct forms
The study of the distribution of species
The study of cell organelles only
mcqs.why: Genetics is defined in the notes as the branch of biology that studies heredity and variation, so this is the correct definition.

mcqs.q: Which factor would cause phenotypic variation among organisms of the same genotype?
options: Exposure to different environments such as food, light, temperature or water
mcqs.why: The notes state that organisms with the same genotype look different under different conditions of food, light, temperature or water, and such environmental variation is not inherited.

mcqs.q: What is a gene?
options: A specific part of DNA that controls one hereditary character
A complete set of chromosomes shown by number and shape
An organism that has undergone mutation
A cross used to find an unknown genotype
mcqs.why: A gene is defined as a specific part of DNA that controls one hereditary character, which distinguishes it from the other terms listed.

mcqs.q: What is an allele?
options: A type of gamete produced by a heterogametic male
An alternative form of a gene present at the same locus on homologous chromosomes
A blended phenotype in a heterozygote
mcqs.why: An allele is an alternative form of a gene present at the same locus on homologous chromosomes, as stated in the lesson notes.

mcqs.q: In Mendel's dihybrid cross RRYY x rryy, what are the F1 plants?
mcqs.why: All F1 plants are heterozygous RrYy with round yellow seeds, showing that round and yellow are dominant over wrinkled and green.

mcqs.q: How many types of gametes does each RrYy parent produce in the dihybrid cross?
options: Four types: RY, Ry, rY and ry
Two types: RY and ry only
Eight types including RR and YY
mcqs.why: Each gene pair segregates and assorts independently, producing four types of gametes from each parent: RY, Ry, rY and ry.

mcqs.q: Why is the law of segregation called the law of purity of gametes?
options: Because only pure homozygous plants were used
Because gametes are formed without meiosis
Because both alleles stay together in each gamete
Because the two alleles separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one allele
mcqs.why: The two alleles separate during gamete formation and each gamete receives only one allele and remains pure, so a gamete never carries both alleles together.

mcqs.q: In the F2 of the dihybrid cross, which phenotypes are the new combinations that prove independent assortment?
mcqs.why: The appearance of the new combinations round green and wrinkled yellow proves the law of independent assortment, because they differ from both parental combinations.

mcqs.q: What is the F2 phenotypic ratio in Mendel's dihybrid cross?
mcqs.why: On self-crossing, F1 gives F2 in the ratio 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green, which is 9:3:3:1.

mcqs.q: What does a monohybrid cross study, compared with a dihybrid cross?
options: Two traits at the same time
One contrasting trait at a time
mcqs.why: A monohybrid cross studies one contrasting trait at a time, whereas a dihybrid cross studies two traits at the same time.

lessons.title: Test Cross and Back Cross
lessons.notes_html:
Test cross

A test cross is a cross of an individual of unknown genotype showing the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual, to find out its genotype.

  • Purpose: to find out the genotype of an individual showing the dominant phenotype.
  • Partner in the cross: a homozygous recessive individual.

Back cross

A back cross is a cross of the F1 hybrid with either of its parents.

CrossDefinition
Test crossAn individual of unknown genotype showing the dominant phenotype crossed with a homozygous recessive individual, to find out its genotype
Back crossThe F1 hybrid crossed with either of its parents

Related terms

  • Mutant: an organism or gene that has undergone a sudden heritable change called mutation.
  • Karyotype: the complete set of chromosomes of a cell shown by number, size and shape.

mcqs.q: In a test cross, the individual of unknown genotype is crossed with which partner?
mcqs.why: A test cross is a cross of an individual of unknown genotype showing the dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual.

mcqs.q: What is the main purpose of a test cross?
options: To find out the genotype of an individual showing the dominant phenotype
To produce a new mutant organism
To count the chromosomes in a karyotype
To cross the F1 hybrid with a parent
mcqs.why: The purpose stated in the notes is to find out the genotype of an individual showing the dominant phenotype by crossing it with a homozygous recessive.

mcqs.q: What is a back cross?
options: A cross between two homozygous recessive individuals
A cross between two different species
A cross that produces only mutants
A cross of the F1 hybrid with either of its parents
mcqs.why: A back cross is defined as a cross of the F1 hybrid with either of its parents, not necessarily with the recessive parent.

mcqs.q: The individual whose genotype is tested in a test cross shows which phenotype?
mcqs.why: A test cross is used for an individual of unknown genotype showing the dominant phenotype, to find out whether it is homozygous or heterozygous.

mcqs.q: What is a mutant?
options: A complete set of chromosomes of a cell
An alternative form of a gene
An organism or gene that has undergone a sudden heritable change called mutation
A gamete carrying only one allele
mcqs.why: A mutant is an organism or gene that has undergone a sudden heritable change called mutation, as defined in the related terms.

mcqs.q: What is a karyotype?
options: The exchange of segments between chromatids
The tendency of genes to be inherited together
A sudden heritable change in a gene
The complete set of chromosomes of a cell shown by number, size and shape
mcqs.why: Karyotype is the complete set of chromosomes of a cell shown by number, size and shape, which is different from linkage, crossing over or mutation.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a test cross from a back cross?
options: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner to reveal genotype; a back cross crosses F1 with either parent
A test cross always uses a parent; a back cross always uses a recessive stranger
Both crosses are exactly the same in partner and purpose
A back cross is only used to find an unknown genotype
mcqs.why: The test cross specifically uses a homozygous recessive partner to find out genotype, while the back cross crosses the F1 hybrid with either of its parents.

mcqs.q: If an F1 hybrid is crossed with its dominant parent, what kind of cross is this?
mcqs.why: Crossing the F1 hybrid with either of its parents, including the dominant parent, is a back cross by definition in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is the partner in a test cross chosen to be homozygous recessive?
options: Because it shows the dominant phenotype most strongly
Because it is the only individual available
Because the cross is defined that way to find out the unknown genotype of the dominant-phenotype individual
mcqs.why: The notes define the test cross by its homozygous recessive partner and its purpose of finding out the genotype of the individual showing the dominant phenotype.

mcqs.q: Which cross would you set up to check the genotype of a plant showing the dominant trait?
options: Cross it with a homozygous recessive individual (a test cross)
Cross it with a homozygous dominant individual
Cross two F1 hybrids with each other only
Cross it with either parent and call it a test cross
mcqs.why: To find out its genotype, the dominant-phenotype individual of unknown genotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive individual, which is a test cross.

lessons.title: Incomplete Dominance
lessons.notes_html:
Incomplete dominance — partial dominance

In incomplete dominance the dominant allele cannot completely suppress the recessive allele in the heterozygote, so the offspring shows a phenotype midway between the two parents. Because dominance is only partial and not complete, it is also called partial dominance.

  • Heterozygote: shows a blended, intermediate phenotype.
  • Example in Mirabilis: pink flowers are produced from red and white parents.

Incomplete dominance and codominance compared

Incomplete dominanceCodominance
The heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotypeBoth alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote, as in blood group AB

mcqs.q: In incomplete dominance, what does the heterozygote show?
options: Both alleles fully and separately expressed
mcqs.why: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotype midway between the two parents.

mcqs.q: Why is incomplete dominance also called partial dominance?
options: Because only part of the flower changes colour
Because it occurs in only some generations
Because the dominant allele cannot completely suppress the recessive allele, so dominance is only partial
Because both alleles are fully expressed
mcqs.why: The dominant allele cannot completely suppress the recessive allele in the heterozygote, so dominance is only partial and not complete, hence partial dominance.

mcqs.q: In Mirabilis, pink flowers are produced from which parents?
mcqs.why: Pink flowers in Mirabilis are produced from red and white parents, with pink being the intermediate heterozygote phenotype.

mcqs.q: What phenotype would the heterozygote have in incomplete dominance between red and white flower colour?
options: Red, because red is fully dominant
Both red and white patches separately
Pink, midway between red and white
mcqs.why: The offspring shows a phenotype midway between the two parents, such as pink flowers from red and white parents in Mirabilis.

mcqs.q: How does incomplete dominance differ from codominance?
options: In codominance the heterozygote is blended; in incomplete dominance both alleles are fully expressed
There is no difference between them
In incomplete dominance neither allele is expressed
In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is blended and intermediate; in codominance both alleles are fully and separately expressed
mcqs.why: Incomplete dominance gives a blended intermediate heterozygote, while in codominance both alleles are fully and separately expressed, as in blood group AB.

mcqs.q: Which example is given for a blended heterozygote phenotype?
options: Blood group AB with both antigens
Pink flowers in Mirabilis from red and white parents
mcqs.why: Pink flowers from red and white parents in Mirabilis are the stated example of the blended, intermediate phenotype of incomplete dominance.

mcqs.q: In incomplete dominance, the recessive allele in the heterozygote is:
options: Completely suppressed with no effect at all
Not completely suppressed, so it affects the intermediate phenotype
Fully expressed on its own as the only phenotype
mcqs.why: The dominant allele cannot completely suppress the recessive allele in the heterozygote, which is why the phenotype is intermediate rather than fully dominant.

mcqs.q: A red-flowered Mirabilis crossed with a white-flowered one gives all pink offspring. This shows:
mcqs.why: Pink offspring midway between red and white parents show incomplete dominance, also called partial dominance, not codominance or complete dominance.

mcqs.q: Which description fits the heterozygote in incomplete dominance?
options: It is identical to the dominant homozygote
It is identical to the recessive homozygote
It expresses both alleles separately without blending
It is midway between the two parental phenotypes
mcqs.why: The heterozygote shows a phenotype midway between the two parents, which is the defining feature of incomplete dominance in the notes.

mcqs.q: Blood group AB is NOT an example of incomplete dominance because:
options: It shows a blended intermediate antigen
Both alleles are fully and separately expressed in it, which is codominance
Neither allele is expressed in it
It has no antigens at all
mcqs.why: Blood group AB is codominance: both alleles are fully and separately expressed, unlike the blended intermediate phenotype of incomplete dominance.

lessons.title: Codominance
lessons.notes_html:
Codominance

In codominance both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote. This is different from incomplete dominance, in which the heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotype.

PatternExpression in the heterozygote
Incomplete dominanceA blended, intermediate phenotype
CodominanceBoth alleles fully and separately expressed

Codominance in the ABO system

In the ABO system, IA and IB are co-dominant to each other. The genotype IAIB gives group AB, in which both antigens A and B are present, so both alleles are expressed together in the same person.

  • IAIB: blood group AB — both antigens A and B are present.
  • Co-dominant male: a male with the co-dominant blood group has group AB (IAIB).

mcqs.q: In codominance, how are the two alleles expressed in the heterozygote?
options: They blend into an intermediate phenotype
Both alleles are fully and separately expressed
mcqs.why: Codominance means both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote, unlike the blended phenotype of incomplete dominance.

mcqs.q: What blood group does the genotype IAIB give?
mcqs.why: The genotype IAIB gives group AB, in which both antigens A and B are present, so both alleles are expressed together in the same person.

mcqs.q: In group AB blood, which antigens are present on the red blood cells?
mcqs.why: Group AB from IAIB has both antigens A and B present, showing that both co-dominant alleles are expressed in the same person.

mcqs.q: IA and IB are described as what in relation to each other?
mcqs.why: In the ABO system IA and IB are co-dominant to each other, and both are dominant over i, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: A male described as having the co-dominant blood group has which group?
mcqs.why: The co-dominant blood group of a male is AB with genotype IAIB, because IA and IB are co-dominant to each other.

mcqs.q: How does codominance differ from incomplete dominance?
options: In codominance both alleles are fully and separately expressed; in incomplete dominance the heterozygote is blended and intermediate
In codominance the heterozygote is blended; in incomplete dominance both are fully expressed
In codominance only the recessive allele is expressed
mcqs.why: Codominance expresses both alleles fully and separately, while incomplete dominance shows a blended, intermediate phenotype in the heterozygote.

mcqs.q: Which genotype shows codominance in the ABO system?
mcqs.why: IAIB shows codominance because IA and IB are co-dominant and both antigens A and B are present in group AB blood.

mcqs.q: If both alleles are fully and separately expressed in a heterozygote, the pattern is called:
mcqs.why: Full and separate expression of both alleles in the heterozygote is the definition of codominance given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: In group AB, the presence of two different antigens shows that:
options: One allele has masked the other completely
The phenotype is a blend midway between A and B
Neither IA nor IB is dominant over i
Both IA and IB are expressed together in the same person
mcqs.why: Both antigens A and B are present in IAIB, so both alleles are expressed together in the same person, which is codominance.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a codominant situation from the notes?
options: Pink flowers from red and white parents
IAIB giving group AB with both antigens present
ii giving group O with no antigen
ee preventing pigment deposition in Labradors
mcqs.why: IAIB giving group AB with both antigens A and B present is the codominance example; pink flowers are incomplete dominance and ii shows no codominance.

lessons.title: Multiple Alleles and Blood Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Multiple alleles

Multiple alleles are three or more alternative forms of the same gene present in a population, such as IA, IB and i for blood groups. Any person carries only two of these alleles.

The ABO blood group system is an example of inheritance explained by multiple alleles on an autosomal chromosome. The ABO gene on an autosome has three alleles, IA, IB and i. Different combinations of these alleles produce blood groups A, B, AB and O.

The ABO blood system

The ABO system is controlled by a single gene with three alleles: IA and IB are co-dominant to each other and both are dominant over i.

Blood groupGenotypeAntigen
AIAIA or IAiA
BIBIB or IBiB
ABIAIBBoth antigens A and B are present
OiiNo antigen
  • Isoagglutinogens: the antigens (A and B) present on the surface of red blood cells that cause agglutination with the opposite antibody.

ABO cross — group A x group B parents

A cross between a group A father (IAi) and a group B mother (IBi) can produce children of all four groups: IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), each with a 25 percent chance. Two parents neither of whom is AB or O can still have AB and O children.

Group A parents with a group O child

A child with blood group O proves that both group A parents are heterozygous, IAi. In the cross IAi x IAi, one out of four children, that is 0.25, receives i from both parents and has blood group O. The probability that the next child will be a boy who has blood group O is 0.25 as printed for this cross.

Codominant AB cross through two generations

The co-dominant blood group of the male is AB (IAIB) and the female is homozygous A (IAIA). Their children receive IA from the mother and either IA or IB from the father, so all their children are either IAIA (group A) or IAIB (group AB), each with 50 percent chance; their male child is therefore either group A (IAIA) or group AB (IAIB).

When this son marries a female with the recessive blood group O (ii), she gives i to every child: if the son is IAIA, all children are IAi, that is 100 percent group A; if the son is IAIB, half the children are IAi (group A) and half are IBi (group B). The grandchildren can only be group A or group B, and group O or AB is not possible in this cross.

Son's genotypeCross with iiChildren
IAIAIAIA x iiAll IAi — 100 percent group A
IAIBIAIB x iiHalf IAi (group A) and half IBi (group B)

Blood group systems

Apart from the well known ABO and Rh systems, the International Society of Blood Transfusion has recognised more than 30 blood group systems in man. Each system is controlled by its own gene or group of genes and its antigens must be considered during transfusion.

Rh incompatibility

An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus may be sensitised by foetal red cells entering her blood at delivery, and she then makes anti-Rh antibodies. In a later pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the red blood cells of an Rh-positive foetus, causing erythroblastosis foetalis, severe anaemia, jaundice and even death of the foetus. Repeated sensitisation also makes transfusion and later pregnancies risky for the mother.

  • Erythroblastosis foetalis: the disease of a newborn Rh-positive baby of an Rh-negative mother, in which maternal anti-Rh antibodies destroy the baby's red blood cells.

mcqs.q: What are multiple alleles?
options: Two alleles carried by every person
Genes present only on the Y chromosome
Three or more alternative forms of the same gene present in a population
mcqs.why: Multiple alleles are three or more alternative forms of the same gene present in a population, such as IA, IB and i for blood groups.

mcqs.q: How many of the ABO alleles does any one person carry?
options: Only two of the three alleles
All three alleles IA, IB and i
mcqs.why: Any person carries only two of the three ABO alleles, even though three alleles IA, IB and i exist in the population.

mcqs.q: The ABO system is an example of multiple alleles on which kind of chromosome?
options: A sex chromosome only in males
mcqs.why: The ABO gene is on an autosome and has three alleles IA, IB and i, so it is multiple alleles on an autosomal chromosome.

mcqs.q: Which genotype gives blood group O and what antigen does it have?
mcqs.why: Genotype ii gives group O with no antigen, while IAIB gives AB, IAi gives A and IBi gives B as shown in the table.

mcqs.q: A person with genotype IAi has which blood group?
mcqs.why: Genotypes IAIA or IAi give group A with antigen A, because IA is dominant over i.

mcqs.q: What are isoagglutinogens?
options: The antigens A and B on the surface of red blood cells that cause agglutination with the opposite antibody
mcqs.why: Isoagglutinogens are the antigens A and B present on the surface of red blood cells that cause agglutination with the opposite antibody.

mcqs.q: How many blood group systems has the International Society of Blood Transfusion recognised in man?
options: Exactly 2 systems, ABO and Rh only
mcqs.why: Apart from ABO and Rh, the International Society of Blood Transfusion has recognised more than 30 blood group systems in man.

mcqs.q: A group A father (IAi) crossed with a group B mother (IBi) can have children of which groups?
options: All four groups: AB, A, B and O, each with 25 percent chance
mcqs.why: IAi x IBi produces IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), each with a 25 percent chance, so all four groups are possible.

mcqs.q: Two group A parents have a daughter of group O. What does this prove about the parents?
options: One parent is actually group AB
The daughter must have a mutation
mcqs.why: A child with group O (ii) proves both group A parents are heterozygous IAi, because each must have passed an i allele to the child.

mcqs.q: In the cross IAi x IAi, what fraction of children receive i from both parents and have group O?
options: One out of two, that is 0.5
Three out of four, that is 0.75
One out of four, that is 0.25
mcqs.why: In IAi x IAi, one out of four children, that is 0.25, receives i from both parents and has blood group O.

mcqs.q: As printed for the IAi x IAi cross in the notes, what is the probability that the next child will be a boy who has blood group O?
mcqs.why: The solved exercise gives the probability as 0.25 for a boy with blood group O in this cross, and the notes repeat that printed value for the IAi x IAi cross.

mcqs.q: A man with group AB (IAIB) marries a woman homozygous for group A (IAIA). Their children will be:
options: Half group B and half group O
Either IAIA (group A) or IAIB (group AB), each with 50 percent chance
mcqs.why: Children receive IA from the mother and either IA or IB from the father, so they are IAIA (group A) or IAIB (group AB), each with 50 percent chance.

mcqs.q: If that AB x homozygous A son with genotype IAIB marries a woman with group O (ii), what are their children?
options: Half group O and half group AB
Half IAi (group A) and half IBi (group B)
mcqs.why: With ii giving i to every child, an IAIB son gives half IAi (group A) and half IBi (group B); group O or AB is not possible in this cross.

mcqs.q: An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus may be sensitised when:
options: Foetal red cells enter her blood at delivery and she then makes anti-Rh antibodies
She receives group O blood in childhood
The foetus makes anti-Rh antibodies against her
She carries a second Rh-negative foetus
mcqs.why: Sensitisation occurs when foetal red cells enter the Rh-negative mother's blood at delivery, after which she makes anti-Rh antibodies that endanger a later Rh-positive foetus.

mcqs.q: Erythroblastosis foetalis is:
options: Complete colour blindness in a newborn
The disease of a newborn Rh-positive baby of an Rh-negative mother, in which maternal anti-Rh antibodies destroy the baby's red blood cells
A disease caused by linked genes
The formation of both antigens A and B
mcqs.why: Erythroblastosis foetalis is the disease of a newborn Rh-positive baby of an Rh-negative mother, in which maternal anti-Rh antibodies destroy the baby's red blood cells, causing severe anaemia and jaundice.

lessons.title: Sex Linkage and Other Inheritance Patterns
lessons.notes_html:
Sex determination in humans

In humans females are XX and males are XY. The mother always passes an X chromosome to the child, while the father passes either X, producing a daughter (XX), or Y, producing a son (XY), so the father's sperm determines the sex of the baby in roughly a 50:50 ratio.

Why the human male is heterogametic

A human male has two different sex chromosomes, X and Y, so during meiosis he produces two types of sperms: half carrying X and half carrying Y. Because he produces more than one type of gamete for sex, the male is called heterogametic, while the female (XX) produces only X-carrying eggs and is homogametic.

Autosomes and sex chromosomes

ChromosomesFeatures
AutosomesAlike in males and females and do not determine sex
Sex chromosomesDiffer between the sexes and determine sex

ZZ and ZW sex determination

In birds, butterflies and some reptiles the sex chromosomes are called Z and W instead of X and Y. The male is homogametic with ZZ chromosomes and produces only Z sperms, while the female is heterogametic with ZW chromosomes and produces Z and W eggs, so in these animals the egg determines the sex of the offspring.

Grasshopper — XX and XO

In grasshopper the female has two X chromosomes (XX) while the male has only one X chromosome (XO) and no second sex chromosome. The female number of chromosomes is 24, and the male therefore has one chromosome less, 23 instead of 24.

X-linked and Y-linked traits

TraitFeatures
X-linked traitControlled by a gene on the X chromosome and can appear in both sexes
Y-linked traitControlled by a gene on the Y chromosome and appears only in males
  • Holandric genes: present only on the non-homologous part of the Y chromosome. They pass directly from father to son only, and are always expressed because males are hemizygous for them.

X-linked inheritance — colour blindness

Genes present on the X chromosome show X-linked inheritance, for example colour blindness: a carrier mother (XN Xn) crossed with a normal father (XN Y) gives normal daughters, half of them carriers, normal sons, and colour-blind sons (Xn Y) in equal proportions. Sons therefore get X-linked recessive disorders from their carrier mothers, while daughters are affected only when they receive the allele from both parents.

  • Colour-blind son: a boy gets his only X chromosome from his mother, so his mother must carry the recessive colour-blind allele n on one X chromosome. A carrier mother XN Xn is phenotypically normal but passes Xn to half of her sons.
  • Parents of a colour-blind son and a non-carrier daughter: the father is normal and the mother is a carrier. The son receives his X chromosome from his mother, so the mother must carry the colour-blind allele. The daughter receives her father's X chromosome, so a normal father gives her a normal X and she is a non-carrier when she also receives a normal X from her mother.
  • Protanopia: red colour blindness, in which a person cannot perceive red colour.
  • Dichromacy: a form of colour blindness in which a person can perceive only two of the three primary colours because one type of cone cells is missing or faulty, for example red blindness (protanopia) or green blindness (deuteranopia).
  • Monochromacy: complete colour blindness, in which the person cannot distinguish colours at all and sees everything in black, white and shades of grey.

Haemophilia

Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder, and a male has only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on that X is expressed and he becomes haemophilic. A female has two X chromosomes, so she is usually only a carrier when one X carries the allele, and she becomes haemophilic only in the rare case when both X chromosomes carry it.

Sex-influenced traits

A sex-influenced trait is an autosomal trait whose expression differs in males and females because of sex hormones, so the same genotype behaves as dominant in one sex and recessive in the other. Pattern baldness in man is a common example: it is dominant in males but recessive in females.

Linkage and crossing over

  • Linkage: the tendency of genes located on the same chromosome to be inherited together.
  • Crossing over: the exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiosis, which produces new combinations.

Linked genes on the same chromosome are inherited together and behave almost like a single gene. That is why a dihybrid cross gives a monohybrid-like 3:1 ratio instead of the usual 9:3:3:1 ratio when the gene loci are linked.

Epistasis — coat colour in Labrador retriever

An epistatic gene present at one locus suppresses or masks the expression of a gene at a different locus. The masked gene is called the hypostatic gene, and this interaction is called epistasis.

Epistasis is the interaction in which a gene at one locus masks the expression of a gene at another locus. In Labrador retrievers, gene B controls the colour of the pigment: BB or Bb gives black coat and bb gives chocolate (brown) coat. Another gene, E, controls whether the pigment is deposited in the fur at all: E allows deposition, but ee prevents it and the dog is yellow, whatever the B genotype.

GenotypeCoat colour
B_E_Black
bbE_Chocolate
B_ee or bbeeYellow

This gives a 9:3:4 ratio in F2 instead of 9:3:3:1. Here gene E is epistatic over gene B.

lessons.title: Evidences of Evolution
lessons.notes_html:
Evolution and special creation

Evolution holds that species change gradually over time and new species arise from earlier ones. Special creation, in contrast, holds that species were created in their present form and do not change. Suarez was a supporter of the theory of special creation, according to which all species were created in their present form by a divine power. Buffon, Lamarck and Darwin, in contrast, presented ideas that supported change in species over time.

Special CreationEvolution
Species were created in their present form and do not changeSpecies change gradually over time and new species arise from earlier ones

Palaeontology — evidence from fossils

Palaeontology, the study of fossils, provides direct historical evidence for evolution. Fossils in older rocks are simpler than those in younger rocks, extinct forms such as dinosaurs are found, and series like the evolution of the horse show step-by-step change from ancestors to modern forms.

  • Older and younger rocks: fossils in older rocks are simpler than those in younger rocks.
  • Extinct forms: extinct forms such as dinosaurs are found as fossils.
  • Step-by-step series: series like the evolution of the horse show gradual change from ancestors to modern forms.

Archaeopteryx — a connecting link

Archaeopteryx is a connecting link between reptiles and Aves (birds). It had reptilian features such as teeth, claws and a long bony tail, along with bird features such as feathers and wings. It therefore links reptiles with birds and shows that birds evolved from reptiles.

  • Reptilian features: teeth, claws and a long bony tail.
  • Bird features: feathers and wings.

Biogeography — evidence from distribution

Biogeography is the study of the distribution of species. Organisms on islands and continents resemble the nearest mainland forms yet differ in a gradual way, such as the finches of the Galapagos Islands, and similar environments on different continents have very different species. This fits descent with modification after continents separated by plate tectonics, not independent creation everywhere. Together, biogeography and palaeontology strongly support evolution.

Homologous organs

Homologous organs have the same basic structure and embryonic origin but perform different functions, such as the forelimbs of man, bat, bird and whale. The wings of bat and bird and the flippers of dolphin are all modified vertebrate forelimbs with the same basic bone pattern, so they are homologous.

Such similarity of plan in different groups can only be explained if they inherited the structure from a common ancestor and then modified it for different uses. This strongly supports evolution and divergent change from common ancestry.

Analogous organs

Analogous organs are organs that perform the same function but have different structure, origin and ancestry, such as the wings of an insect and the wings of a bird. Both are used for flying, but the insect wing is a chitinous outgrowth without bones, while the bird wing is a modified forelimb with bones. Their similarity is due to convergent evolution under similar conditions, not common ancestry.

The wings of an insect, a bird and a bat perform the same function of flight but have different structure and origin, so they are analogous to each other. The arm of man is not a flight organ and is homologous, not analogous, to the vertebrate wings. The wing of a butterfly is made of chitin and has no vertebrate bones, so it is not homologous with the wings of bat and bird or the flippers of dolphin.

Homologous OrgansAnalogous Organs
Same basic structure and embryonic origin, different functionsSame function, different structure, origin and ancestry
Forelimbs of man, bat, bird and whale; wings of bat and bird and flippers of dolphin as modified vertebrate forelimbsWings of insect and wings of bird; wings of insect, bird and bat for flight
Show common ancestry and divergent changeShow convergent evolution under similar conditions

Convergent and divergent evolution

  • Convergent evolution: unrelated organisms develop similar features because of similar environments.
  • Divergent evolution: related organisms develop different features from a common ancestor.

lessons.title: Theories of Evolution — Lamarckism, Darwinism and Neo-Darwinism
lessons.notes_html:
Lamarck and Philosophie Zoologique

Jean Baptiste de Lamarck published his theory of evolution in his book Philosophie Zoologique in 1809. In it he proposed the inheritance of acquired characters through use and disuse of organs. Lamarck presented the first systematic theory of organic evolution in this book, known as Lamarckism or the theory of inheritance of acquired characters.

Lamarckism — main ideas

  • New needs: a changing environment creates new needs in organisms.
  • Use of organs: organs which are used more become stronger and larger; continuously using some organ results in its further strengthening in offspring, in Lamarck's proposal.
  • Disuse of organs: disused organs weaken and may disappear; continuously disusing some organ results in its weakening in offspring, in Lamarck's proposal.
  • Inheritance of acquired characters: characters acquired during life are inherited by the offspring.
  • Example: the long neck of the giraffe, developed by stretching to reach high leaves.

Limits of Lamarckism

Lamarck's ideas about use, disuse and strengthening or weakening of organs in the offspring were his proposed explanation, but they were never supported by concrete experimental evidence. Later experiments, such as those of Weismann, showed that characters acquired during life are not inherited. His mechanism was later disproved.

Lamarck as an early proponent of evolution

Lamarck was one of the first scientists to propose, in 1809, a complete theory that species are not fixed but change over time to become better adapted to their environment. Although his explanation of inheritance of acquired characters was later rejected, he introduced the ideas of gradual change, adaptation and use and disuse, and prepared the way for Darwin. His contribution remains important because he first established that species change gradually, that adaptation is related to the environment, and that evolution proceeds from simple to complex forms. He is therefore rightly regarded as an early proponent of evolution.

Lamarckism and Darwinism

LamarckismDarwinism
Explains evolution by use and disuse of organs and inheritance of acquired charactersExplains evolution by variation and natural selection of the fittest

Darwinism and genetics

Darwin supported natural selection with evidence from biogeography, comparative anatomy and fossils, but he did not know the mechanism of heredity. Genetics was not developed in his time, so his theory lacked genetic support until Neo-Darwinism combined it with genetics. Darwinism explains evolution mainly by natural selection acting on variations, but Darwin could not explain the origin and inheritance of variations.

Neo-Darwinism

Neo-Darwinism is the modern form of the theory that adds genetics. Variations arise by mutation and recombination, are stored in the gene pool of a population, and natural selection, genetic drift and isolation change allele frequencies to produce new species.

DarwinismNeo-Darwinism
Explains evolution mainly by natural selection acting on variations; origin and inheritance of variations not explainedAdds genetics — variations arise by mutation and recombination and are stored in the gene pool
No genetic support in Darwin's timeNatural selection, genetic drift and isolation change allele frequencies to produce new species

lessons.title: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection
lessons.notes_html:
Malthus and the struggle for existence

Thomas Malthus proposed that human population increases faster than its food supply, so many individuals must die in the struggle for existence. Darwin applied this idea to all species and developed the idea of survival of the fittest through natural selection. The theory on human population which inspired Darwin was proposed by Malthus.

Observations behind natural selection

  • Overproduction: organisms produce far more offspring than can survive.
  • Limited resources: resources are limited, so there is a struggle for existence.
  • Variation: individuals of a population show heritable variations.
  • Unequal fitness: organisms are not all equally fit for their environment.

Theory of natural selection

Individuals with variations favourable for that environment survive and reproduce more successfully — survival of the fittest — and pass their useful characters to their offspring, while the less fit are gradually eliminated. Continued over many generations, this natural selection accumulates favourable variations and produces new, better adapted species.

Chain: overproduction → struggle for existence → heritable variation → survival of the fittest → useful characters passed to offspring → accumulation over many generations → new, better adapted species.

Descent with modification

Descent with modification is Darwin's phrase for evolution: present-day species have descended, with gradual changes, from pre-existing ancestral species. Over long periods these small inherited modifications accumulate, producing organisms that are different from their ancestors and, in time, entirely new species. The process of natural selection producing new species is the process Darwin called descent with modification.

Alfred Wallace and natural selection

Alfred Russel Wallace, working independently in the Malay Archipelago, reached the same idea of natural selection as Darwin and sent his essay to Darwin in 1858. This contribution pushed Darwin to finally publish his work, and their papers were presented together, after which Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859. Wallace also contributed greatly through his studies of the geographical distribution of animals.

EventDetail
Wallace's workReached the same idea of natural selection independently in the Malay Archipelago
1858Wallace sent his essay to Darwin; their papers were presented together
1859Darwin published On the Origin of Species

lessons.title: Population Genetics — Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium and Genetic Drift
lessons.notes_html:
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium stays undisturbed when mating is random, there is no selection, no mutation, no migration and the population is large. Selection, non-random mating and mutation change allele frequencies, so they disrupt the equilibrium, while random mating does not. Random mating therefore cannot be a disruptive force for the Hardy-Weinberg theorem.

  • Conditions for equilibrium: random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration and a large population.
  • Disruptive forces: selection, non-random mating and mutation change allele frequencies and disrupt the equilibrium.

Factors affecting allele frequency

The main factors that change allele frequency in a population are mutation, natural selection, genetic drift, gene flow and non-random mating. Gene flow is the migration of individuals in or out of the population. Any of these factors disturbs the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and can lead to evolution of the population over generations.

  • Mutation
  • Natural selection
  • Genetic drift
  • Gene flow: migration of individuals in or out of the population.
  • Non-random mating

Genetic drift

Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies in a population from one generation to the next, occurring purely by chance. It is strongest in small populations, where a few individuals breeding or dying by chance can greatly change or even eliminate an allele, as seen in the bottleneck and founder effects.

Bottleneck effect and founder effect

Bottleneck EffectFounder Effect
A disaster greatly reduces the size of a population and its genetic variationA small group separates from a large population and starts a new population with a different gene pool

Both effects are examples of genetic drift, in which allele frequencies change by chance, with the strongest effects in small populations.

lessons.title: Origin of Life, Origin of Eukaryotes and Speciation
lessons.notes_html:
Origin of life in water

The first life forms originated in water, especially in shallow seas and hot springs called hydrothermal vents. Water provided the medium in which simple chemicals combined to form complex organic compounds and the first cells.

Origin of single-celled eukaryotes

Single-celled eukaryotes arose from prokaryotic ancestors more than about 1.5 billion years ago in water. These changes gave the first single-celled eukaryotes a nucleus, organelles and greater efficiency, from which all later eukaryotic life evolved.

Invagination theory

According to the invagination theory, the cell membrane of a prokaryote folded inwards and enclosed the genetic material, forming a true nucleus and internal membranes such as the endoplasmic reticulum. The invagination theory says eukaryotic organelles formed when the prokaryotic cell membrane folded inwards to enclose the genetic material.

Endosymbiotic theory

According to the endosymbiotic theory, larger prokaryotic cells engulfed smaller aerobic bacteria, which were not digested but lived inside them in symbiosis and became mitochondria, and photosynthetic cyanobacteria similarly became chloroplasts. The endosymbiotic theory says mitochondria and chloroplasts arose from free-living bacteria that were taken inside another cell and lived in symbiosis.

Invagination TheoryEndosymbiotic Theory
Eukaryotic organelles formed when the prokaryotic cell membrane folded inwards to enclose the genetic material; this formed a true nucleus and internal membranes such as the endoplasmic reticulumMitochondria and chloroplasts arose from free-living bacteria taken inside another cell and living in symbiosis; aerobic bacteria became mitochondria and photosynthetic cyanobacteria became chloroplasts

Speciation

Speciation is the biological process by which one or more new species are formed from an existing species when populations become reproductively isolated and accumulate genetic differences.

Allopatric speciation

In allopatric speciation, a geographical barrier such as a river, mountain or sea separates a population, and the separated parts evolve independently into new species.

Sympatric speciation

In sympatric speciation a new species arises within the same geographical area, without any physical barrier, often through polyploidy or a change in habits or mating time. A new species arises in the same area, for example by polyploidy in plants or a change in food, habitat or breeding season.

Parapatric speciation

In parapatric speciation a new species arises in a population that lives in neighbouring, partly overlapping areas, where gene flow is limited and the two ends of the range gradually become different species. Neighbouring populations in adjoining areas with limited gene flow gradually diverge into separate species.

lessons.title: Ecosystem Producers and Ecological Succession
lessons.notes_html:
Major producers in a terrestrial ecosystem

The major producers in a terrestrial ecosystem are green plants, including grasses, herbs, shrubs and trees, which make food by photosynthesis. All other organisms of the ecosystem depend directly or indirectly on them for food and energy.

  • In a forest: the trees are the chief producers.
  • In grassland: the grasses play the role of chief producers.

Ecological succession

Succession is the gradual and directional process by which the community of an area changes over time until a stable climax community is formed. Simple pioneer species are replaced step by step by more complex and larger species through seral stages.

Succession increases the diversity, biomass and stability of the community and finally produces a climax community that is in balance with the climate of the area.

Pioneers in xerarch succession

Xerarch succession starts on dry bare rock. Crustose lichens are the first, pioneer organisms to grow there. They slowly break the rock surface and help in soil formation, preparing the way for mosses and higher plants.

Secondary succession

Secondary succession occurs where a community has been disturbed but soil and some organisms remain, for example a burnt forest or an abandoned cultivated field. Because soil is already present, secondary succession is much faster than primary succession.

  • Stage 1: annual weeds and grasses grow first.
  • Stage 2: perennial herbs and shrubs appear.
  • Stage 3: fast-growing softwood trees such as pine appear.
  • Final stage: hardwood trees form the climax forest.

Chain: disturbed area with soil remaining → annual weeds and grasses → perennial herbs and shrubs → softwood trees such as pine → hardwood climax forest.

lessons.title: Biogeochemical Cycles — Meaning and Types
lessons.notes_html:
What a biogeochemical cycle is

A biogeochemical cycle is the repeated circulation of an element, such as carbon or nitrogen, between living organisms and the non-living environment, so that the element is used again and again.

Why it is called biogeochemical

It is called biogeochemical because the elements involved move in a cycle through living organisms (bio), the Earth and soil (geo) and chemical changes in air and water (chemical). For example, nitrogen passes from air to soil, into plants and animals, and back to air through the activities of living organisms and chemical processes.

  • Bio: living organisms.
  • Geo: the Earth and soil.
  • Chemical: chemical changes in air and water.

Gaseous and sedimentary cycles

Carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles are gaseous cycles because their main reservoir is the atmosphere or oceans. The phosphorus cycle is not a gaseous type of cycle: in the phosphorus cycle the main reservoir is rocks and soil, not the atmosphere, so it is a sedimentary cycle.

CycleTypeMain reservoir
Carbon cycleGaseousAtmosphere or oceans
Nitrogen cycleGaseousAtmosphere or oceans
Oxygen cycleGaseousAtmosphere or oceans
Phosphorus cycleSedimentaryRocks and soil

Source of carbon to plants

The source of carbon to plants in the carbon cycle is atmospheric carbon dioxide. Green plants take carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere for photosynthesis and convert it into food. From plants this carbon passes to animals and other organisms through food chains.

lessons.title: The Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
The nitrogen cycle in detail

Atmospheric nitrogen is about 78 percent of air. It is first fixed into compounds by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and in the root nodules of legumes, by lightning and by industry, forming ammonia and nitrates.

  • Nitrogen fixation: atmospheric nitrogen is fixed into compounds by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and in the root nodules of legumes, by lightning and by industry, forming ammonia and nitrates.
  • Use by plants and animals: plants absorb nitrates and make proteins, and animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants.
  • Ammonification: the dead bodies and wastes of organisms are broken down by decomposers into ammonia.
  • Nitrification: nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and nitrates, which plants absorb again.
  • Denitrification: denitrifying bacteria convert some nitrates back into free nitrogen gas, completing the cycle.

Chain: atmospheric nitrogen → fixation → ammonia and nitrates → plant proteins → animals → dead bodies and wastes → ammonia by ammonification → nitrites and nitrates by nitrification → plants again, with some nitrates returned to free nitrogen by denitrification.

Nitrification and denitrification compared

NitrificationDenitrification
Conversion of ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates by nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas and NitrobacterDenitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into free nitrogen gas, which escapes into the atmosphere
Makes nitrogen available to plants in the soilReduces soil fertility

Denitrification is the conversion of nitrates to nitrogen. It is the reverse of nitrification, in which ammonia is converted into nitrites and nitrates.

Nitrogen balance and proteins

Nitrogen enters the body mainly through proteins in food and is lost mainly in urea in urine. Nitrogen balance compares this intake and loss of nitrogen, so it depends directly on the amount of protein eaten. The dietary requirement involved in nitrogen balance is therefore proteins.

lessons.title: Energy Flow Through Food Chains and Food Webs
lessons.notes_html:
The Sun — source of energy for ecosystems

Solar energy is the ultimate and only original source of energy for almost all ecosystems on Earth. Producers capture it by photosynthesis, and from them energy flows to all consumers through food chains.

How energy flows between trophic levels

Energy flows in one direction only, from producers to herbivores, then to carnivores and finally to decomposers, through food chains and food webs.

Chain: producers → herbivores → carnivores → decomposers.

  • Passed on: at each transfer only about 10 percent of the energy is passed on.
  • Lost or used: the rest is lost as heat, used in life activities or left in undigested material.
  • Result: higher trophic levels receive much less energy.

Heat loss at each trophic level

Heat loss is a factor that affects the flow of energy at the trophic level. At every trophic level a large part of the energy is lost as heat during respiration and other life activities. Because of this heat loss, only about 10 percent of the energy of one trophic level passes to the next level.

At one trophic levelShare of energy
Passed to the next trophic levelAbout 10 percent
Lost as heat, used in life activities, or left in undigested materialThe rest

Processes that absorb heat energy

Melting of ice and evaporation of water absorb heat energy from the surroundings, so the energy change for these processes is positive (endothermic). Such processes take in energy instead of releasing it.

lessons.title: Global Warming, Ozone Depletion, Population and Conservation
lessons.notes_html:
The greenhouse effect and global warming

The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat in the atmosphere by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, and its increase is seen as global warming. As the Earth becomes warmer, ice melts, sea level rises and weather patterns change.

Rise of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere

The main cause of the increase in the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is the burning of a large number of fossil fuels. Burning of coal, oil and gas in vehicles, factories and power houses releases huge amounts of carbon dioxide into the air. This is the main cause of the steady rise of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and of the greenhouse effect.

Effects of carbon dioxide and global warming on human health

  • Heat illness: higher temperatures cause heat strokes and dehydration, especially in old people and outdoor workers.
  • Infectious diseases: warmer and wetter conditions help mosquitoes and other vectors spread, increasing malaria, dengue and other infectious diseases.
  • Food and water: global warming disturbs rainfall and agriculture, causing food shortages and malnutrition.
  • Displacement: melting ice and rising sea level displace coastal populations.
  • Breathing problems: increased air pollution and allergens along with warming worsen asthma and other breathing problems.

Causes of ozone layer depletion

The main cause of ozone layer depletion is the release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in refrigerators, air conditioners, sprays and foams. Other ozone-destroying substances include halons, carbon tetrachloride and nitrogen oxides from jet planes and fertilisers. In the upper atmosphere these release chlorine, which breaks down ozone molecules and thins the protective ozone layer.

Factors that determine the growth rate of the human population

The growth rate of the human population is determined mainly by birth rate and death rate, and also by immigration and emigration. Improvements in agriculture, industry and control of diseases are the reasons why death rate has fallen much faster than birth rate, causing rapid population growth.

FactorEffect and reason
Birth rateA high birth rate increases population because more children are added
Death rateBetter medical facilities, sanitation and food supply have reduced the death rate, so people live longer and population grows faster
ImmigrationIncreases the population of the area people move into
EmigrationDecreases the population of the area people leave

Why biodiversity should be conserved

Biodiversity provides food, medicines, fibres and many other useful products and maintains ecosystem services such as pollination, soil formation, water purification and balance of gases in the air. Loss of species can collapse food webs and make ecosystems unstable, so conserving biodiversity is essential for human survival and well-being.

lessons.title: Tools of Biotechnology — Restriction Enzymes, PCR, Gel Electrophoresis and Blotting
lessons.notes_html:
Restriction enzymes as molecular scissors

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences, just as scissors cut at a chosen point. Each enzyme recognises its own specific sequence and cuts both strands there, often producing sticky ends. Because they cut DNA molecules precisely at desired sites for joining with other DNA, they are called molecular scissors.

Palindromic sequences in DNA

A palindrome in DNA is a sequence of bases that reads the same on both strands when read in the 5 to 3 direction, like the word MADAM reads the same from both sides.

  • Example: the sequence GAATTC on one strand pairs with CTTAAG on the other and reads GAATTC in both directions.
  • Recognition sites: restriction enzymes recognise and cut such palindromic sequences.

Polymerase chain reaction — PCR

PCR is a technique used to amplify DNA. It makes millions of copies of a small DNA sample, providing enough DNA for sequencing.

  • Sequencing: the amplified DNA provides enough material for sequencing.
  • Identifying genetic disorders: the amplified DNA is used to identify genetic disorders.
  • Gene expression: in its reverse-transcriptase form, PCR is used to study gene expression.

Gel electrophoresis

Gel electrophoresis is a technique used to separate DNA fragments based on size. DNA fragments move through the gel at different speeds according to their size, forming bands that can be compared between samples. Differences in band patterns reveal genetic variations, which is used in DNA fingerprinting and diagnosis.

Southern blotting

Southern blotting is a technique used to transfer DNA fragments from a gel to a membrane. DNA fragments fixed on a membrane are detected with a labelled probe that binds to a specific sequence. This detects mutations and abnormal gene fragments, so it is used to identify genetic disorders.

lessons.title: DNA Sequencing, DNA Analysis and Genomic Maps
lessons.notes_html:
DNA sequencing

DNA sequencing is the technique of determining the exact order of nucleotides (A, T, G and C) in a DNA molecule. By reading the exact order of nucleotides, sequencing reveals changes or mutations in DNA when a sequence is compared with a normal reference sequence. These identified variations help in diagnosing genetic diseases and in studying differences between individuals and species.

Sanger sequencing

Sanger sequencing determines the exact order of nucleotides in a DNA fragment by using chain-terminating nucleotides. It was the standard method used to sequence genes and even whole genomes, including in the Human Genome Project. DNA sequencing is most commonly done by the Sanger method, using chain-terminating nucleotides and gel electrophoresis.

Sequencing and the study of genetic mutations and diseases

To study a disease, the gene of a patient is sequenced and compared with the normal sequence; any change, such as substitution, deletion or insertion of bases, identifies the mutation causing the disorder, as in cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia and many cancers.

  • Carrier detection: sequencing has allowed carrier detection.
  • Prenatal diagnosis: sequencing has allowed prenatal diagnosis.
  • Disease genes: sequencing allowed discovery of disease genes through the Human Genome Project.
  • Treatment: sequencing allows the choice of suitable treatment for individual patients.

DNA analysis

DNA analysis examines a sample of DNA to detect variations, mutations or specific markers present in it. Finding such variations makes it possible to identify genetic disorders, carriers of a disease and relationships between individuals.

Genomic maps

A genomic map shows the positions of genes and other markers on all the chromosomes of an organism. By comparing maps of healthy and diseased persons, scientists can locate and identify the genes responsible for specific diseases.

Creating a genomic map

  • Genetic linkage map: created first, in which the distance between markers is estimated from how often they are separated by crossing over in families.
  • Physical map: created next, in which overlapping DNA fragments are cloned, cut with restriction enzymes and sequenced to fix their exact positions in base pairs.

Genomic maps, completed for man in the Human Genome Project, have been used to locate disease genes such as those for cystic fibrosis and Huntington disease, to identify carriers, to compare genomes of different species and to develop new diagnostic tests and gene-based medicines.
